# Overview

Ketamine produces analgesia and sedation via NMDA receptor antagonism and complex interactions with cholinergic, dopaminergic, glutamatergic, histaminergic, and GABAergic systems, which can unmask or precipitate delirium in vulnerable patients. <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Ketamine’s pharmacology is dose-dependent, with analgesic predominance at 0.1–0.4 mg/kg/hr and sedative/hallucinatory effects at higher doses (0.4–1.0 mg/kg/hr), and psychotic/hallucinatory symptoms become common at ≥1 mg/kg/hr</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-4">As an NMDA receptor antagonist, ketamine’s dissociative state resembles catatonia and amnesia and is associated with dose‑related hallucinations and psychosis</cite>. <cite id="e3bd9592-0">At the systems level, neurotransmitter imbalances—reduced acetylcholine and serotonin, excess glutamate, dopaminergic excess, and altered histamine/GABA/norepinephrine—are central to delirium pathophysiology, and ketamine can modulate these and has anti‑inflammatory and neuroprotective properties</cite>.

Across clinical settings, ketamine exposure is variably associated with delirium. <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">In critically ill adults receiving ICU analgosedation, ketamine exposure was associated with increased incident ICU delirium, with median exposure around 0.5 mg/kg/hr and higher ketamine doses linked to more psychiatric symptoms</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-3">In perioperative contexts, small cohorts and reviews have reported both reductions and increases in postoperative delirium with ketamine; notably, a large randomized trial in elderly patients undergoing major surgery found no difference in delirium incidence and a tendency toward more hallucinations and nightmares</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-0">In pediatric anesthesia/ED, emergence delirium is common, with risk factors including young age, substance use, certain surgical types, opioid exposure, and benzodiazepine premedication</cite>, while targeted strategies such as prophylactic haloperidol or ketamine adjuncts may alter behavioral outcomes in specific scenarios <cite id="bd35304d-1">prophylactic haloperidol reduced agitation/disorientation and increased calm/sleepy behaviors in pediatric patients after ketamine</cite> and <cite id="bd35304d-2">adding ketamine to caudal blocks prolonged emergence time and analgesia and eliminated the need for ED medication in one randomized pediatric study</cite>.

# Mechanisms Linking Ketamine and Delirium

Multiple, interacting mechanisms explain why ketamine can precipitate or modulate delirium:

- Glutamatergic/NMDA and network-level effects: <cite id="7c0f2f88-4">By antagonizing NMDA receptors, ketamine induces a dissociative state with catatonia, amnesia, and dose‑related hallucinations and psychosis</cite>. <cite id="e3bd9592-0">Ketamine’s modulation of neurotransmitter release may counteract excess glutamate and support cholinergic/serotonergic balance, potentially mitigating delirium in some contexts</cite>. <cite id="e3bd9592-0">In cardiac surgery, perioperative ketamine (0.5 mg/kg) was associated with reduced postoperative delirium and lower CRP, suggesting anti‑inflammatory mediation</cite>.

- Cholinergic and dopaminergic pathways: <cite id="e3bd9592-2">Delirium commonly involves decreased cholinergic activity and dopaminergic excess; anticholinergic medications precipitate delirium and haloperidol (a potent dopamine antagonist) can be therapeutic</cite>. <cite id="e3bd9592-3">Central cholinergic deficiency, excess dopamine, and changes in serotonin, histamine, and GABA are repeatedly implicated in delirium, interacting with arousal/consciousness networks</cite>.

- Neuroinflammation and oxidative stress: <cite id="7c0f2f88-2">Ketamine exposure correlates with psychotic/hallucinatory symptoms at higher doses</cite>, and <cite id="e3bd9592-0">ketamine exhibits anti‑inflammatory and neuroprotective properties that may reduce delirium risk in inflammatory states</cite>. <cite id="e3bd9592-4">In ICU delirium, oxidative stress, neurotransmitter dysfunction, and neuroinflammation are intertwined; triggers like infection and surgical trauma increase inflammatory markers and ROS, compromising the blood–brain barrier and promoting neurotoxicity</cite>.

- Dose, timing, and clinical milieu: <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Lower-dose ketamine (0.1–0.4 mg/kg/hr) is primarily analgesic, whereas 0.4–1.0 mg/kg/hr produces sedation and hallucinations become common at ≥1 mg/kg/hr</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-4">Dose-related psychotomimetic effects mirror delirium phenotypes, and ICU comorbidity, coma, opioid and benzodiazepine exposure potentiate risk</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Age, coma, and opioid/benzodiazepine use independently increase delirium risk in ketamine‑exposed ICU patients</cite>.

# Clinical Associations by Setting

## Critically Ill Adults (ICU Analgosedation)

Prospective cohort evidence suggests a contribution of ketamine to incident ICU delirium:

- <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">In a single-center cohort of nearly 1,000 critically ill adults, ketamine analgosedation was associated with increased incident delirium; median ketamine dose at onset of delirium was 0.5 mg/kg/hr, and psychiatric symptoms (psychosis/hallucinations) were frequent at ≥1 mg/kg/hr</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-2">Similar motoric subtype profiles, treatments (restraints, antipsychotics, dexmedetomidine), and outcomes between ketamine and non‑ketamine delirium groups suggest comparable severity, with ketamine patients more often on opioids and IV clonidine</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-1">However, small sample of ketamine users, wide confidence intervals, variable prescribing practices, unclear dose–duration effects, and unmeasured confounders limited precision and causal inference</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-3">The authors conclude ketamine analgosedation may increase delirium risk and call for prospective randomized trials</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-4">They contextualize ketamine’s dissociative and dose‑related psychotomimetic effects and note similarities to delirium phenotypes</cite>.

- Mechanistic alignment and mixed comparative literature: <cite id="7c0f2f88-4">Ketamine’s neuropharmacology and delirium’s neurotransmitter derangements align, but prior randomized trials and cohorts have shown inconsistent delirium effects</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Lower-dose ketamine regimens used in Perbert et al. (fixed low-dose infusion ~2.5× lower than that in ketamine patients who developed delirium here) reported fewer delirium events and less opioid exposure</cite>.

## Perioperative Adults

Effects of intraoperative or perioperative ketamine on postoperative delirium are inconsistent:

- <cite id="bd35304d-3">Small prospective work in cardiac surgery reported a 30% reduction in postoperative delirium with perioperative ketamine; however, a multicenter randomized trial in elderly patients (n=672) found no significant difference in delirium incidence and a trend toward more hallucinations and nightmares, noting ketamine’s NMDA and HCN1 antagonism</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-3">A systematic review summarized six studies: two decreases, one increase, one equivocal, and two with no delirium patients, underscoring heterogeneity</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-3">Some surgical services adopt intraoperative ketamine to reduce opioid-induced delirium, but evidence remains limited and mixed</cite>.

## Pediatric Emergence (Anesthesia/ED)

- <cite id="bd35304d-0">In elective pediatric surgery, emergence delirium occurred in 55.6% of 99 patients; risk factors included age 18–25 years, smoking, alcoholism, certain surgical specialties (ophthalmology), alprazolam premedication, general anesthesia/ETT exposure, longer operative time, and opioid use</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-1">Prophylactic haloperidol before ketamine reduced emergence agitation/disorientation and increased calm/sleepy behaviors in children</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-2">As a caudal analgesia adjunct, ketamine prolonged emergence time and analgesia and eliminated the need for ED medication in a randomized pediatric study</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-4">Ketamine was more effective than midazolam in reducing emergence agitation and decreased rescue analgesia with earlier PACU discharge in sevoflurane anesthesia</cite>. These data suggest ketamine can both increase acute psychomimetic disturbances and be harnessed with adjunctive pharmacology to blunt emergence delirium/agitation when carefully titrated.

# Risk Modifiers and Dose/Timing Effects

- Dose and infusion rate: <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Psychotic/hallucinatory symptoms are most common at ≥1 mg/kg/hr; sedative effects and delirium risk increase at 0.4–1.0 mg/kg/hr compared with lower analgesic doses</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Median ketamine dose at onset of delirium in ICU patients was 0.5 mg/kg/hr</cite>.

- Comorbid neurologic illness and sedative co-exposure: <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Coma, opioid use, and benzodiazepine use independently increased delirium risk in ketamine-exposed ICU cohorts</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-0">Benzodiazepine (alprazolam) premedication and opioid exposure were independent risk factors for emergence delirium in pediatric surgery</cite>. <cite id="e3bd9592-2">Anticholinergic medications precipitate delirium and dopamine antagonism can treat it, underscoring the cholinergic–dopaminergic axis</cite>.

- Age and inflammation: <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Older age was a delirium risk in ICU cohorts</cite>, and <cite id="e3bd9592-0">ketamine’s potential anti‑inflammatory effects may reduce delirium in inflammatory states like cardiac surgery (associated with CRP reduction)</cite>. Conversely, <cite id="bd35304d-3">a large RCT in elderly major-surgery patients showed no delirium reduction and more hallucinations/nightsmares</cite>, highlighting that anti‑inflammatory properties do not guarantee clinical benefit and may have adverse cognitive-affective side effects.

- Timing and illness severity: <cite id="7c0f2f88-1">Uncertainty persists about whether early vs later ICU admission-to-ketamine initiation affects delirium risk, due to variable prescribing practices and limited data on daily ABCDEF bundle use</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">High-dose exposure and co-exposure to coma and benzodiazepines are salient modifiers</cite>. <cite id="e3bd9592-4">Neuroinflammation/oxidative stress from acute illness and injury are upstream drivers of delirium and interact with neuromodulator dysfunction</cite>.

# Delirium Subtypes and Clinical Presentation

- Phenotypic overlap: <cite id="7c0f2f88-4">Ketamine’s dissociative, catatonic, amnestic, and hallucinatory states closely mimic delirium presentations, especially at higher doses</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-2">ICU delirium subtypes and treatment needs (restraints, antipsychotics, dexmedetomidine) were similar between ketamine and non‑ketamine delirium groups, suggesting comparable motoric involvement</cite>. <cite id="e3bd9592-2">Delirium subtype frameworks implicate prefrontal–cingulate–basal ganglia and parietal–thalamic networks with cholinergic hypoactivity and dopaminergic excess</cite>.

- Pediatric emergence: <cite id="bd35304d-2">Emergence delirium is often agitated/hallucinatory; in one pediatric trial, ketamine as a caudal adjunct did not require ED medication, implying possible subtype shifting from agitated to painful delirium</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-1">Haloperidol prophylaxis decreased disorientation and agitation</cite>.

- Inflammatory triggers: <cite id="e3bd9592-0">Surgical trauma elevates CRP and ROS, disrupts the blood–brain barrier, and contributes to delirium; ketamine’s anti-inflammatory properties may attenuate this pathway</cite>.

# Management and Prevention Strategies

- Dose selection and vigilance: <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Limit ketamine to analgesic ranges (≤0.4 mg/kg/hr) when possible, escalate cautiously for sedation (0.4–1.0 mg/kg/hr) with close monitoring, and avoid ≥1 mg/kg/hr where clinically unnecessary due to increased hallucinations/psychosis</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">At 0.5 mg/kg/hr, ICU patients had high rates of incident delirium in a dose‑matched cohort</cite>.

- Reduce co-exposures and anticholinergic burden: <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Avoid benzodiazepines and minimize opioids when feasible; both independently increase delirium risk alongside ketamine</cite>. <cite id="e3bd9592-2">Given anticholinergic drugs precipitate delirium and dopamine antagonism can treat it, prioritize cholinergic support and minimize benzodiazepine exposure</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-0">Alprazolam premedication increased emergence delirium risk in pediatric surgery</cite>.

- Pharmacologic mitigation:
  - Adjunctive sedation/antipsychotics: <cite id="7c0f2f88-2">Dexmedetomidine, haloperidol, and restraints were used similarly across ketamine and non‑ketamine delirium groups when delirium occurred</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-1">Prophylactic haloperidol reduced agitation/disorientation after pediatric ketamine</cite>.
  - Closed-loop sedation and opioid/benzodiazepine control: <cite id="7c0f2f88-1">The study noted lack of standardized delirium prevention bundles (e.g., ABCDEF) and variable sedation practices; consistent protocols may reduce risk</cite>.
  - Ketamine as adjunct to regional anesthesia: <cite id="bd35304d-2">Caudal ketamine prolonged emergence time and analgesia and eliminated the need for ED medication in one randomized pediatric study</cite>.

- Procedural/ED settings: <cite id="bd35304d-1">Haloperidol prophylaxis before ketamine reduced emergence delirium/agitation metrics in children</cite>, and <cite id="bd35304d-4">ketamine outperformed midazolam for emergence agitation and reduced rescue analgesia with earlier discharge in pediatric sevoflurane anesthesia</cite>. These findings support titration, co‑administration strategies, and early ondansetron/haloperidol prophylaxis pathways to preempt delirium phenotypes in ED settings.

- Inflammatory/oxidative contexts: <cite id="e3bd9592-0">Perioperative cardiac surgery data linked ketamine to lower CRP and reduced delirium in some cohorts, suggesting anti‑inflammatory benefit; however, RCT evidence in elderly major surgery showed no delirium reduction and more hallucinations/nightsmares</cite>. Thus, anti‑inflammatory adjuncts (e.g., adequate analgesia to minimize stress responses, early infection source control) remain foundational, and ketamine’s role should be weighed against psychotomimetic side effects.

# Special Populations and Use Cases

- Elderly patients: <cite id="e3bd9592-0">In elderly ICU patients (>60 years), neither 0.5 nor 1 mg/kg ketamine reduced delirium incidence in a randomized trial; ketamine groups had more hallucinations and nightmares</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Age independently increased delirium risk in ketamine-exposed ICU adults</cite>. Given polypharmacy and cholinergic vulnerability, careful dose selection and anticholinergic minimization are essential.

- Pediatric anesthesia: <cite id="bd35304d-0">Emergence delirium is common with risk factors including young age, substance use, certain surgical types, benzodiazepines, and opioids</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-1">Haloperidol prophylaxis decreased disorientation and agitation after ketamine</cite>, and <cite id="bd35304d-2">ketamine as a caudal adjunct can reduce ED need for intervention</cite>.

- Transition from opioid-dominant to ketamine-enhanced multimodal analgesia: <cite id="bd35304d-3">Some services transition postoperatively to ketamine-based regimens to reduce opioid-induced delirium, but evidence remains mixed and the American Pain Society cautions due to hallucinations/nightsmares</cite>.

# Practical Recommendations (Evidence-Informed)

- Choose low-dose ketamine for analgesia first and titrate for sedation only when necessary; target ≤0.4 mg/kg/hr for analgesia and escalate cautiously to 0.4–0.8 mg/kg/hr for sedation with frequent reassessment, avoiding ≥1 mg/kg/hr unless for specific indications, given strong associations with hallucinations/psychosis and incident ICU delirium at intermediate doses <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Ketamine’s dose–response for psychotomimetic effects favors lower-to-moderate ranges</cite> and <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">psychotic/hallucinatory symptoms are common at ≥1 mg/kg/hr</cite>.

- Minimize benzodiazepines and cumulative anticholinergic burden; if benzodiazepines are required, keep durations short and consider cholinergic support (e.g., maintaining euglycemia, hydration, avoiding anticholinergic agents). <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Benzodiazepine and opioid exposure independently increase delirium risk in ketamine-exposed ICU patients</cite> and <cite id="e3bd9592-2">anticholinergic exposure precipitates delirium</cite>.

- In perioperative settings, consider ketamine as part of multimodal analgesia to reduce opioids, but monitor for emergence and postoperative delirium. Use prophylactic antipsychotics or ondansetron/haloperidol pathways in ED/anesthesia to preempt agitation/delirium; consider ketamine adjuncts to regional anesthesia to prolong analgesia and reduce ED need for pharmacologic calm. <cite id="bd35304d-1">Haloperidol prophylaxis improved calm/sleepy behaviors and reduced disorientation after pediatric ketamine</cite> and <cite id="bd35304d-2">ketamine as caudal adjunct eliminated ED medication in one RCT</cite>.

- For ICU analgosedation, adopt closed-loop sedation, daily delirium screening, early mobilization, and benzodiazepine tapering; if ketamine is used, document dose, duration, and titrate to minimal effective levels, and have rapid access to antipsychotics/dexmedetomidine for breakthrough delirium. <cite id="7c0f2f88-1">The cohort highlighted wide CIs and variable prescribing; standardized protocols and ABCDEF bundle integration could mitigate risk</cite> and <cite id="7c0f2f88-2">treatments for delirium (restraints, antipsychotics, dexmedetomidine) were similar across ketamine and non‑ketamine delirium groups</cite>.

- In inflammatory states (cardiac surgery, sepsis), ketamine’s anti‑inflammatory properties may help, but do not guarantee delirium prevention; balance anti‑inflammatory benefit against psychotomimetic side effects by optimizing adjunctive care (early pain control, infection control, metabolic stabilization). <cite id="e3bd9592-0">Perioperative CRP reduction with ketamine was associated with delirium reduction in cardiac surgery cohorts, but RCTs in elderly major surgery showed no delirium reduction and more hallucinations/nightsmares</cite>.

# Key Uncertainties and Research Needs

- Causality and dose–response: <cite id="7c0f2f88-1">Prospective ICU analyses face small ketamine samples, variable prescribing, and unclear dose–duration effects, limiting causal inference</cite>. Randomized trials with careful delirium phenotyping and biomarker integration are needed to quantify risk across dose ranges and illness severities <cite id="7c0f2f88-3">Future well-designed, prospective, randomized trials are required to determine the magnitude of delirium risk and whether ICU ketamine delirium truly represents delirium</cite>.

- Setting-specific risk estimates: <cite id="bd35304d-3">Perioperative evidence is mixed, with reductions in some cardiac cohorts but no benefit and more hallucinations in elderly major surgery</cite>, underscoring heterogeneity by surgery type, dose, and comorbidity. Multicenter pragmatic trials stratified by age, surgical specialty, and baseline delirium risk are needed.

- Mechanism-directed prevention: While cholinergic hypoactivity and neuroinflammation are implicated, clinical translation remains limited. Trials of cholinesterase inhibitors, histamine H3 antagonists, or ketamine regimens paired with anti-inflammatory and metabolic stabilization strategies could clarify prevention pathways <cite id="e3bd9592-2">Cholinergic deficiency and neuroinflammation/oxidative stress are central but incompletely translated into clinical prevention</cite>.

# Bottom Line

Ketamine can precipitate delirium—particularly at higher sedative doses and in the presence of coma, benzodiazepines, and opioids—but in selected inflammatory contexts may reduce delirium via anti‑inflammatory mechanisms; its psychotomimetic side effects necessitate careful dose selection, minimized co‑exposures, and proactive delirium prevention. <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">In critically ill adults, ketamine analgosedation was associated with increased incident delirium at median doses around 0.5 mg/kg/hr, with psychotic/hallucinatory symptoms common at ≥1 mg/kg/hr</cite> and <cite id="7c0f2f88-4">its NMDA-mediated dissociation closely resembles delirium phenotypes</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-3">Perioperative effects are mixed; an RCT in elderly major surgery found no delirium reduction and more hallucinations/nightsmares</cite>, whereas <cite id="e3bd9592-0">in cardiac surgery, perioperative ketamine has been linked to lower CRP and reduced delirium in some cohorts</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-1">Prophylactic haloperidol can reduce emergence delirium/agitation after pediatric ketamine</cite>, and <cite id="bd35304d-2">ketamine as a regional adjunct may reduce the need for ED medication</cite>. Clinicians should individualize dosing, minimize anticholinergic burden, and integrate daily delirium screening and closed-loop sedation, recognizing ketamine’s dual potential to mitigate or precipitate delirium depending on dose, setting, and comorbidity. <cite id="7c0f2f88-1">Current evidence is limited by variable prescribing practices and small ketamine samples, and rigorous randomized trials with standardized delirium prevention bundles are needed</cite>.

Title: Exploring Ketamine Analgosedation Use and Its Effect on Incident Delirium in Critically Ill Adults
Snippet: Our results suggest ketamine, when administered to critically ill surgical and medical patients requiring analgosedation, may increase the risk for ICU incident delirium. Age, coma, opioid use, and benzodiazepine use were also each independently associated with a greater delirium risk. With the exception that patients admitted to the ICU for urgent surgery were more likely to develop delirium with ketamine and more ketamine patients with delirium received opioid and IV clonidine therapy, other delirium risks, motorotic subtypes, treatments, and ICU outcomes were similar between the ketamine and nonketamine patients who developed delirium. 

Ketamine, with its lack of effect on respiratory drive and low propensity to cause hypotension or coma, has advantages over opioids and propofol in critically ill adults requiring analgosedation (1, 2). Ketamine is increasingly being used to optimize ICU patient comfort and safety (3) despite the current lack of a large, multicenter, controlled trial evaluating its analgosedation safety and efficacy (3). Title: Exploring Ketamine Analgosedation Use and Its Effect on Incident Delirium in Critically Ill Adults
Snippet: Our study has important strengths. We evaluated close to 1,000 adults who were critically ill (median APACHE-IV score = 67), prospectively collected data on both ketamine use and common delirium risk variables, rigorously evaluated both delirium and coma tid, and ensured patients with delirium prior to ketamine initiation were excluded. We then evaluated the risk of ketamine for incident delirium in a regression model that accounted for delirium risk variables that were different between the delirium and nondelirium groups (4). 

Our study also has limitations. The number of patients in our cohort who received ketamine was low; ketamine analgosedation is most often used in patients with high sedative needs. The wide CIs that surround the odds ratios for delirium risk we present weaken the precision of our findings. A consistent approach for ketamine analgosedation prescribing was not in place throughout the study; the specific prescribing rationale for ketamine initiation and titration was not known. The high proportion of ketamine patients who developed incident delirium precluded determining whether the ketamine dose or infusion duration affects this risk. Delirium risk factors not included in our analysis may have affected our results. For patients having delirium prior to or on the same day of ketamine initiation, the contributory effect of ketamine to delirium occurrence remains unknown. 

We were not able to consider whether the time from ICU admission to ketamine initiation affects delirium risk. The results of our single-hospital analysis may be different in ICUs where ketamine prescribing practices are different, patients have different delirium risks, or delirium prevention and treatment strategies are different or unavailable (e.g., IV clonidine). Some of the delirium treatment strategies may have been used for nondelirium treatment indications (e.g., haloperidol for postoperative nausea and vomiting). We did not collect data on daily ABCDEF bundle use.
</snippet>

We carefully considered common ICU delirium risk factors and compared delirium characteristics, treatments, and outcomes between the ketamine and no-ketamine patients who developed ICU incident delirium. Title: Exploring Ketamine Analgosedation Use and Its Effect on Incident Delirium in Critically Ill Adults
Snippet: K etamine, an anesthetic with both analgesic and sedative properties, is increasingly being used in both surgical and medical critically ill adults for analgosedation (1)(2)(3). Delirium, a common sequela of critical illness, is associated with poor outcomes (4). Medications, including benzodiazepines (5) and opioids (6), are well-established risk factors for delirium in the ICU. Ketamine, an N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor antagonist, results in a dissociative state clinically manifesting as catatonia and amnesia, and is associated in a dose-dependent fashion with hallucinations and psychosis (7). Similarities exist between the clinical effects of ketamine and the symptoms of delirium (4). 

One randomized trial (8) and four cohort studies (9)(10)(11)(12) have evaluated delirium in critically ill adults managed with ketamine analogosedation. In the randomized trial (8), the ketamine dose administered was low and fixed, and compared with the placebo group, the ketamine group received fewer opioids, an important dose-related risk for delirium (6). None of the ICU cohort studies reported a difference in delirium with ketamine use (9)(10)(11)(12). Title: Does haloperidol prophylaxis reduce ketamine-induced emergence delirium in children?
Snippet: OBJECTIVES
Ketamine is a non-barbiturate agent with rapid action onset that induces profound sedation; however, some emergency physicians tend not to use ketamine because of the risk of emergence delirium (ED). This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of haloperidol prophylaxis in postoperative ketamine delirium in children.


METHODS
Prospective data relating to any emergence dreams, delirium, hallucinations, agitation, crying, altered perceptions, and necessary interventions were recorded in consecutive cases of ketamine delirium in patients attending Mansoura University Hospital, Egypt, from June 2010 to May 2011.


RESULTS
A total of 537 records were available for analysis. Of those, 267 received prophylactic haloperidol (49.7%). There were significant differences between the two groups regarding post-anaesthetic care unit behaviour. The ketamine-haloperidol groups included more patients who were sleepy, calm (P ≤0.01) and less irritable (P ≤0.01), with a lower incidence of crying (P ≤0.01) and disorientation (P ≤0.01).


CONCLUSION
We found that preoperative administration of haloperidol decreases the incidence of postoperative delirium in a sample of Egyptian children undergoing minor surgery. This is congruent with earlier work conducted in adults. This work carries great hope to decrease and even prevent ED in hospitalised, non-surgical patients.
</snippet>

Title: Caudal block and emergence delirium in pediatric patients: Is it analgesia or sedation?
Snippet: Background: Emergence delirium (ED) although a short-lived and self-limiting phenomenon, makes a child prone to injury in the immediate postoperative period and hence is a cause of concern not only to the pediatric anesthesiologist, surgeons, and post anesthesia care unit staff but also amongst parents. Additional medication to quieten the child offsets the potential benefits of rapid emergence and delays recovery in day care settings. There is conflicting evidence of influence of analgesia and sedation following anesthesia on emergence agitation. We hypothesized that an anesthetic technique which improves analgesia and prolongs emergence time will reduce the incidence of ED. We selected ketamine as adjuvant to caudal block for this purpose. Methods: This randomized, double blind prospective study was performed in 150 premedicated children ASA I, II, aged 2 to 8 years who were randomly assigned to either group B (caudal with bupivacaine), BK (bupivacaine and ketamine), or NC (no caudal), soon after LMA placement. Recovery characteristics and complications were recorded. Results: Emergence time, duration of pain relief, and Pediatric Anesthesia Emergence Delirium (PAED) scores were significantly higher in the NC group (P<0.05). Duration of analgesia and emergence time were significantly more in group BK than groups B and NC. However, the discharge readiness was comparable between all groups. No patient in BK group required to be given any medication to treat ED. Conclusion: Emergence time as well as duration of analgesia have significant influence on incidence of emergence delirium. Ketamine, as caudal adjuvant is a promising agent to protect against ED in children, following sevoflurane anesthesia.
</snippet>

Disturbance in the synthesis and release of neurotransmitters, such as reduced cholinergic and serotonergic activity and excess release of glutamate, can lead to functional connectivity alteration of neurons, resulting in atrophy and brain damage, which play crucial roles in delirium development (47)(48)(49)(50)(51). Ketamine has been shown to balance these neurotransmitter releases in the brain (52)(53)(54). Moreover, the beneficial effect of ketamine on preventing delirium might be due to its anti-inflammatory properties (27), neuroprotective activity (55), and anti-depressant properties (56). A study by Hudetz et al. on elderly patients undergoing cardiac surgery showed that the injection of 0.5 mg/kg of ketamine during the anesthesia decreased the incidence of postoperative delirium. The reduction in delirium was associated with a decrease in serum C-reactive protein (CRP) concentrations, suggesting the anti-inflammatory function of ketamine (29). 

Inflammation plays a significant role in the development of delirium, as indicated by previous studies (57,58). Surgical trauma, for instance, can trigger an elevation in inflammatory markers, such as CRP, which can subsequently promote the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). These ROS have the potential to induce disruption of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and contribute to the onset of delirium (57). Ketamine's anti-inflammatory properties might contribute to its potential in reducing delirium through several mechanisms.

Snippet: Delirium commonly occurs among patients hospitalized in the intensive care unit (ICU). Along with the direct physiological consequences of general medical conditions, delirium is an independent predictor of poor outcomes, including prolonged ICU and hospital stay, low quality of life, and increased mortality (1)(2)(3)(4)(5). In this light, it is necessary to identify reliable and easily accessible biomarkers to improve the recognition and early detection of delirium (6,7). 

The underlying pathophysiology of delirium remains unclear due to the cumulative effect of multiple interconnecting results (4,(8)(9)(10). To date, several theories have been proposed to elucidate the development of delirium (11). Each proposed theory has focused on a specific mechanism of pathologic process, observational, and empirical evidence (11). The oxidative stress hypothesis asserts that a high brain oxidation metabolic rate and a low antioxidant capacity may increase damage to the brain tissue, leading to the development of persistent delirium (12). The decreased brain oxidative metabolism also results in abnormalities in various neurotransmitter systems, causing brain dysfunction and the behavioral symptoms of delirium (10). In the neurotransmitter hypothesis, the dysfunction of neurotransmitters associated with cholinergic and dopaminergic systems, such as reduced availability of acetylcholine, excess discharge of dopamine, norepinephrine, and/or glutamate, and alterations in serotonin, histamine, and/or gamma-aminobutyric acid, would lead to delirium (10,13). In fact, some of the major triggers for cholinergic hypoactivity have long been recognized as the underlying cause of delirium (14). Imbalance and changes in neurotransmitters are also associated with neuroinflammatory processes (10,15). 

According to the neuroinflammatory hypothesis, the neuroinflammation and immune responses due to acute injury or extensive physical stress may result in delirium (11,16).

# Overview

Ketamine produces analgesia and sedation via NMDA receptor antagonism and complex interactions with cholinergic, dopaminergic, glutamatergic, histaminergic, and GABAergic systems, which can unmask or precipitate delirium in vulnerable patients. <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Ketamine’s pharmacology is dose-dependent, with analgesic predominance at 0.1–0.4 mg/kg/hr and sedative/hallucinatory effects at higher doses (0.4–1.0 mg/kg/hr), and psychotic/hallucinatory symptoms become common at ≥1 mg/kg/hr</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-4">As an NMDA receptor antagonist, ketamine’s dissociative state resembles catatonia and amnesia and is associated with dose‑related hallucinations and psychosis</cite>. <cite id="e3bd9592-0">At the systems level, neurotransmitter imbalances—reduced acetylcholine and serotonin, excess glutamate, dopaminergic excess, and altered histamine/GABA/norepinephrine—are central to delirium pathophysiology, and ketamine can modulate these and has anti‑inflammatory and neuroprotective properties</cite>.

Across clinical settings, ketamine exposure is variably associated with delirium. <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">In critically ill adults receiving ICU analgosedation, ketamine exposure was associated with increased incident ICU delirium, with median exposure around 0.5 mg/kg/hr and higher ketamine doses linked to more psychiatric symptoms</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-3">In perioperative contexts, small cohorts and reviews have reported both reductions and increases in postoperative delirium with ketamine; notably, a large randomized trial in elderly patients undergoing major surgery found no difference in delirium incidence and a tendency toward more hallucinations and nightmares</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-0">In pediatric anesthesia/ED, emergence delirium is common, with risk factors including young age, substance use, certain surgical types, opioid exposure, and benzodiazepine premedication</cite>, while targeted strategies such as prophylactic haloperidol or ketamine adjuncts may alter behavioral outcomes in specific scenarios <cite id="bd35304d-1">prophylactic haloperidol reduced agitation/disorientation and increased calm/sleepy behaviors in pediatric patients after ketamine</cite> and <cite id="bd35304d-2">adding ketamine to caudal blocks prolonged emergence time and analgesia and eliminated the need for ED medication in one randomized pediatric study</cite>.

# Mechanisms Linking Ketamine and Delirium

Multiple, interacting mechanisms explain why ketamine can precipitate or modulate delirium:

- Glutamatergic/NMDA and network-level effects: <cite id="7c0f2f88-4">By antagonizing NMDA receptors, ketamine induces a dissociative state with catatonia, amnesia, and dose‑related hallucinations and psychosis</cite>. <cite id="e3bd9592-0">Ketamine’s modulation of neurotransmitter release may counteract excess glutamate and support cholinergic/serotonergic balance, potentially mitigating delirium in some contexts</cite>. <cite id="e3bd9592-0">In cardiac surgery, perioperative ketamine (0.5 mg/kg) was associated with reduced postoperative delirium and lower CRP, suggesting anti‑inflammatory mediation</cite>.

- Cholinergic and dopaminergic pathways: <cite id="e3bd9592-2">Delirium commonly involves decreased cholinergic activity and dopaminergic excess; anticholinergic medications precipitate delirium and haloperidol (a potent dopamine antagonist) can be therapeutic</cite>. <cite id="e3bd9592-3">Central cholinergic deficiency, excess dopamine, and changes in serotonin, histamine, and GABA are repeatedly implicated in delirium, interacting with arousal/consciousness networks</cite>.

- Neuroinflammation and oxidative stress: <cite id="7c0f2f88-2">Ketamine exposure correlates with psychotic/hallucinatory symptoms at higher doses</cite>, and <cite id="e3bd9592-0">ketamine exhibits anti‑inflammatory and neuroprotective properties that may reduce delirium risk in inflammatory states</cite>. <cite id="e3bd9592-4">In ICU delirium, oxidative stress, neurotransmitter dysfunction, and neuroinflammation are intertwined; triggers like infection and surgical trauma increase inflammatory markers and ROS, compromising the blood–brain barrier and promoting neurotoxicity</cite>.

- Dose, timing, and clinical milieu: <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Lower-dose ketamine (0.1–0.4 mg/kg/hr) is primarily analgesic, whereas 0.4–1.0 mg/kg/hr produces sedation and hallucinations become common at ≥1 mg/kg/hr</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-4">Dose-related psychotomimetic effects mirror delirium phenotypes, and ICU comorbidity, coma, opioid and benzodiazepine exposure potentiate risk</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Age, coma, and opioid/benzodiazepine use independently increase delirium risk in ketamine‑exposed ICU patients</cite>.

# Clinical Associations by Setting

## Critically Ill Adults (ICU Analgosedation)

Prospective cohort evidence suggests a contribution of ketamine to incident ICU delirium:

- <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">In a single-center cohort of nearly 1,000 critically ill adults, ketamine analgosedation was associated with increased incident delirium; median ketamine dose at onset of delirium was 0.5 mg/kg/hr, and psychiatric symptoms (psychosis/hallucinations) were frequent at ≥1 mg/kg/hr</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-2">Similar motoric subtype profiles, treatments (restraints, antipsychotics, dexmedetomidine), and outcomes between ketamine and non‑ketamine delirium groups suggest comparable severity, with ketamine patients more often on opioids and IV clonidine</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-1">However, small sample of ketamine users, wide confidence intervals, variable prescribing practices, unclear dose–duration effects, and unmeasured confounders limited precision and causal inference</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-3">The authors conclude ketamine analgosedation may increase delirium risk and call for prospective randomized trials</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-4">They contextualize ketamine’s dissociative and dose‑related psychotomimetic effects and note similarities to delirium phenotypes</cite>.

- Mechanistic alignment and mixed comparative literature: <cite id="7c0f2f88-4">Ketamine’s neuropharmacology and delirium’s neurotransmitter derangements align, but prior randomized trials and cohorts have shown inconsistent delirium effects</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Lower-dose ketamine regimens used in Perbert et al. (fixed low-dose infusion ~2.5× lower than that in ketamine patients who developed delirium here) reported fewer delirium events and less opioid exposure</cite>.

## Perioperative Adults

Effects of intraoperative or perioperative ketamine on postoperative delirium are inconsistent:

- <cite id="bd35304d-3">Small prospective work in cardiac surgery reported a 30% reduction in postoperative delirium with perioperative ketamine; however, a multicenter randomized trial in elderly patients (n=672) found no significant difference in delirium incidence and a trend toward more hallucinations and nightmares, noting ketamine’s NMDA and HCN1 antagonism</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-3">A systematic review summarized six studies: two decreases, one increase, one equivocal, and two with no delirium patients, underscoring heterogeneity</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-3">Some surgical services adopt intraoperative ketamine to reduce opioid-induced delirium, but evidence remains limited and mixed</cite>.

## Pediatric Emergence (Anesthesia/ED)

- <cite id="bd35304d-0">In elective pediatric surgery, emergence delirium occurred in 55.6% of 99 patients; risk factors included age 18–25 years, smoking, alcoholism, certain surgical specialties (ophthalmology), alprazolam premedication, general anesthesia/ETT exposure, longer operative time, and opioid use</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-1">Prophylactic haloperidol before ketamine reduced emergence agitation/disorientation and increased calm/sleepy behaviors in children</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-2">As a caudal analgesia adjunct, ketamine prolonged emergence time and analgesia and eliminated the need for ED medication in a randomized pediatric study</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-4">Ketamine was more effective than midazolam in reducing emergence agitation and decreased rescue analgesia with earlier PACU discharge in sevoflurane anesthesia</cite>. These data suggest ketamine can both increase acute psychomimetic disturbances and be harnessed with adjunctive pharmacology to blunt emergence delirium/agitation when carefully titrated.

# Risk Modifiers and Dose/Timing Effects

- Dose and infusion rate: <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Psychotic/hallucinatory symptoms are most common at ≥1 mg/kg/hr; sedative effects and delirium risk increase at 0.4–1.0 mg/kg/hr compared with lower analgesic doses</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Median ketamine dose at onset of delirium in ICU patients was 0.5 mg/kg/hr</cite>.

- Comorbid neurologic illness and sedative co-exposure: <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Coma, opioid use, and benzodiazepine use independently increased delirium risk in ketamine-exposed ICU cohorts</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-0">Benzodiazepine (alprazolam) premedication and opioid exposure were independent risk factors for emergence delirium in pediatric surgery</cite>. <cite id="e3bd9592-2">Anticholinergic medications precipitate delirium and dopamine antagonism can treat it, underscoring the cholinergic–dopaminergic axis</cite>.

- Age and inflammation: <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Older age was a delirium risk in ICU cohorts</cite>, and <cite id="e3bd9592-0">ketamine’s potential anti‑inflammatory effects may reduce delirium in inflammatory states like cardiac surgery (associated with CRP reduction)</cite>. Conversely, <cite id="bd35304d-3">a large RCT in elderly major-surgery patients showed no delirium reduction and more hallucinations/nightsmares</cite>, highlighting that anti‑inflammatory properties do not guarantee clinical benefit and may have adverse cognitive-affective side effects.

- Timing and illness severity: <cite id="7c0f2f88-1">Uncertainty persists about whether early vs later ICU admission-to-ketamine initiation affects delirium risk, due to variable prescribing practices and limited data on daily ABCDEF bundle use</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">High-dose exposure and co-exposure to coma and benzodiazepines are salient modifiers</cite>. <cite id="e3bd9592-4">Neuroinflammation/oxidative stress from acute illness and injury are upstream drivers of delirium and interact with neuromodulator dysfunction</cite>.

# Delirium Subtypes and Clinical Presentation

- Phenotypic overlap: <cite id="7c0f2f88-4">Ketamine’s dissociative, catatonic, amnestic, and hallucinatory states closely mimic delirium presentations, especially at higher doses</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-2">ICU delirium subtypes and treatment needs (restraints, antipsychotics, dexmedetomidine) were similar between ketamine and non‑ketamine delirium groups, suggesting comparable motoric involvement</cite>. <cite id="e3bd9592-2">Delirium subtype frameworks implicate prefrontal–cingulate–basal ganglia and parietal–thalamic networks with cholinergic hypoactivity and dopaminergic excess</cite>.

- Pediatric emergence: <cite id="bd35304d-2">Emergence delirium is often agitated/hallucinatory; in one pediatric trial, ketamine as a caudal adjunct did not require ED medication, implying possible subtype shifting from agitated to painful delirium</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-1">Haloperidol prophylaxis decreased disorientation and agitation</cite>.

- Inflammatory triggers: <cite id="e3bd9592-0">Surgical trauma elevates CRP and ROS, disrupts the blood–brain barrier, and contributes to delirium; ketamine’s anti-inflammatory properties may attenuate this pathway</cite>.

# Management and Prevention Strategies

- Dose selection and vigilance: <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Limit ketamine to analgesic ranges (≤0.4 mg/kg/hr) when possible, escalate cautiously for sedation (0.4–1.0 mg/kg/hr) with close monitoring, and avoid ≥1 mg/kg/hr where clinically unnecessary due to increased hallucinations/psychosis</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">At 0.5 mg/kg/hr, ICU patients had high rates of incident delirium in a dose‑matched cohort</cite>.

- Reduce co-exposures and anticholinergic burden: <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Avoid benzodiazepines and minimize opioids when feasible; both independently increase delirium risk alongside ketamine</cite>. <cite id="e3bd9592-2">Given anticholinergic drugs precipitate delirium and dopamine antagonism can treat it, prioritize cholinergic support and minimize benzodiazepine exposure</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-0">Alprazolam premedication increased emergence delirium risk in pediatric surgery</cite>.

- Pharmacologic mitigation:
  - Adjunctive sedation/antipsychotics: <cite id="7c0f2f88-2">Dexmedetomidine, haloperidol, and restraints were used similarly across ketamine and non‑ketamine delirium groups when delirium occurred</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-1">Prophylactic haloperidol reduced agitation/disorientation after pediatric ketamine</cite>.
  - Closed-loop sedation and opioid/benzodiazepine control: <cite id="7c0f2f88-1">The study noted lack of standardized delirium prevention bundles (e.g., ABCDEF) and variable sedation practices; consistent protocols may reduce risk</cite>.
  - Ketamine as adjunct to regional anesthesia: <cite id="bd35304d-2">Caudal ketamine prolonged emergence time and analgesia and eliminated the need for ED medication in one randomized pediatric study</cite>.

- Procedural/ED settings: <cite id="bd35304d-1">Haloperidol prophylaxis before ketamine reduced emergence delirium/agitation metrics in children</cite>, and <cite id="bd35304d-4">ketamine outperformed midazolam for emergence agitation and reduced rescue analgesia with earlier discharge in pediatric sevoflurane anesthesia</cite>. These findings support titration, co‑administration strategies, and early ondansetron/haloperidol prophylaxis pathways to preempt delirium phenotypes in ED settings.

- Inflammatory/oxidative contexts: <cite id="e3bd9592-0">Perioperative cardiac surgery data linked ketamine to lower CRP and reduced delirium in some cohorts, suggesting anti‑inflammatory benefit; however, RCT evidence in elderly major surgery showed no delirium reduction and more hallucinations/nightsmares</cite>. Thus, anti‑inflammatory adjuncts (e.g., adequate analgesia to minimize stress responses, early infection source control) remain foundational, and ketamine’s role should be weighed against psychotomimetic side effects.

# Special Populations and Use Cases

- Elderly patients: <cite id="e3bd9592-0">In elderly ICU patients (>60 years), neither 0.5 nor 1 mg/kg ketamine reduced delirium incidence in a randomized trial; ketamine groups had more hallucinations and nightmares</cite>. <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Age independently increased delirium risk in ketamine-exposed ICU adults</cite>. Given polypharmacy and cholinergic vulnerability, careful dose selection and anticholinergic minimization are essential.

- Pediatric anesthesia: <cite id="bd35304d-0">Emergence delirium is common with risk factors including young age, substance use, certain surgical types, benzodiazepines, and opioids</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-1">Haloperidol prophylaxis decreased disorientation and agitation after ketamine</cite>, and <cite id="bd35304d-2">ketamine as a caudal adjunct can reduce ED need for intervention</cite>.

- Transition from opioid-dominant to ketamine-enhanced multimodal analgesia: <cite id="bd35304d-3">Some services transition postoperatively to ketamine-based regimens to reduce opioid-induced delirium, but evidence remains mixed and the American Pain Society cautions due to hallucinations/nightsmares</cite>.

# Practical Recommendations (Evidence-Informed)

- Choose low-dose ketamine for analgesia first and titrate for sedation only when necessary; target ≤0.4 mg/kg/hr for analgesia and escalate cautiously to 0.4–0.8 mg/kg/hr for sedation with frequent reassessment, avoiding ≥1 mg/kg/hr unless for specific indications, given strong associations with hallucinations/psychosis and incident ICU delirium at intermediate doses <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Ketamine’s dose–response for psychotomimetic effects favors lower-to-moderate ranges</cite> and <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">psychotic/hallucinatory symptoms are common at ≥1 mg/kg/hr</cite>.

- Minimize benzodiazepines and cumulative anticholinergic burden; if benzodiazepines are required, keep durations short and consider cholinergic support (e.g., maintaining euglycemia, hydration, avoiding anticholinergic agents). <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">Benzodiazepine and opioid exposure independently increase delirium risk in ketamine-exposed ICU patients</cite> and <cite id="e3bd9592-2">anticholinergic exposure precipitates delirium</cite>.

- In perioperative settings, consider ketamine as part of multimodal analgesia to reduce opioids, but monitor for emergence and postoperative delirium. Use prophylactic antipsychotics or ondansetron/haloperidol pathways in ED/anesthesia to preempt agitation/delirium; consider ketamine adjuncts to regional anesthesia to prolong analgesia and reduce ED need for pharmacologic calm. <cite id="bd35304d-1">Haloperidol prophylaxis improved calm/sleepy behaviors and reduced disorientation after pediatric ketamine</cite> and <cite id="bd35304d-2">ketamine as caudal adjunct eliminated ED medication in one RCT</cite>.

- For ICU analgosedation, adopt closed-loop sedation, daily delirium screening, early mobilization, and benzodiazepine tapering; if ketamine is used, document dose, duration, and titrate to minimal effective levels, and have rapid access to antipsychotics/dexmedetomidine for breakthrough delirium. <cite id="7c0f2f88-1">The cohort highlighted wide CIs and variable prescribing; standardized protocols and ABCDEF bundle integration could mitigate risk</cite> and <cite id="7c0f2f88-2">treatments for delirium (restraints, antipsychotics, dexmedetomidine) were similar across ketamine and non‑ketamine delirium groups</cite>.

- In inflammatory states (cardiac surgery, sepsis), ketamine’s anti‑inflammatory properties may help, but do not guarantee delirium prevention; balance anti‑inflammatory benefit against psychotomimetic side effects by optimizing adjunctive care (early pain control, infection control, metabolic stabilization). <cite id="e3bd9592-0">Perioperative CRP reduction with ketamine was associated with delirium reduction in cardiac surgery cohorts, but RCTs in elderly major surgery showed no delirium reduction and more hallucinations/nightsmares</cite>.

# Key Uncertainties and Research Needs

- Causality and dose–response: <cite id="7c0f2f88-1">Prospective ICU analyses face small ketamine samples, variable prescribing, and unclear dose–duration effects, limiting causal inference</cite>. Randomized trials with careful delirium phenotyping and biomarker integration are needed to quantify risk across dose ranges and illness severities <cite id="7c0f2f88-3">Future well-designed, prospective, randomized trials are required to determine the magnitude of delirium risk and whether ICU ketamine delirium truly represents delirium</cite>.

- Setting-specific risk estimates: <cite id="bd35304d-3">Perioperative evidence is mixed, with reductions in some cardiac cohorts but no benefit and more hallucinations in elderly major surgery</cite>, underscoring heterogeneity by surgery type, dose, and comorbidity. Multicenter pragmatic trials stratified by age, surgical specialty, and baseline delirium risk are needed.

- Mechanism-directed prevention: While cholinergic hypoactivity and neuroinflammation are implicated, clinical translation remains limited. Trials of cholinesterase inhibitors, histamine H3 antagonists, or ketamine regimens paired with anti-inflammatory and metabolic stabilization strategies could clarify prevention pathways <cite id="e3bd9592-2">Cholinergic deficiency and neuroinflammation/oxidative stress are central but incompletely translated into clinical prevention</cite>.

# Bottom Line

Ketamine can precipitate delirium—particularly at higher sedative doses and in the presence of coma, benzodiazepines, and opioids—but in selected inflammatory contexts may reduce delirium via anti‑inflammatory mechanisms; its psychotomimetic side effects necessitate careful dose selection, minimized co‑exposures, and proactive delirium prevention. <cite id="7c0f2f88-0">In critically ill adults, ketamine analgosedation was associated with increased incident delirium at median doses around 0.5 mg/kg/hr, with psychotic/hallucinatory symptoms common at ≥1 mg/kg/hr</cite> and <cite id="7c0f2f88-4">its NMDA-mediated dissociation closely resembles delirium phenotypes</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-3">Perioperative effects are mixed; an RCT in elderly major surgery found no delirium reduction and more hallucinations/nightsmares</cite>, whereas <cite id="e3bd9592-0">in cardiac surgery, perioperative ketamine has been linked to lower CRP and reduced delirium in some cohorts</cite>. <cite id="bd35304d-1">Prophylactic haloperidol can reduce emergence delirium/agitation after pediatric ketamine</cite>, and <cite id="bd35304d-2">ketamine as a regional adjunct may reduce the need for ED medication</cite>. Clinicians should individualize dosing, minimize anticholinergic burden, and integrate daily delirium screening and closed-loop sedation, recognizing ketamine’s dual potential to mitigate or precipitate delirium depending on dose, setting, and comorbidity. <cite id="7c0f2f88-1">Current evidence is limited by variable prescribing practices and small ketamine samples, and rigorous randomized trials with standardized delirium prevention bundles are needed</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Exploring Ketamine Analgosedation Use and Its Effect on Incident Delirium in Critically Ill Adults
Snippet: Our results suggest ketamine, when administered to critically ill surgical and medical patients requiring analgosedation, may increase the risk for ICU incident delirium. Age, coma, opioid use, and benzodiazepine use were also each independently associated with a greater delirium risk. With the exception that patients admitted to the ICU for urgent surgery were more likely to develop delirium with ketamine and more ketamine patients with delirium received opioid and IV clonidine therapy, other delirium risks, motorotic subtypes, treatments, and ICU outcomes were similar between the ketamine and nonketamine patients who developed delirium. 

Ketamine, with its lack of effect on respiratory drive and low propensity to cause hypotension or coma, has advantages over opioids and propofol in critically ill adults requiring analgosedation (1, 2). Ketamine is increasingly being used to optimize ICU patient comfort and safety (3) despite the current lack of a large, multicenter, controlled trial evaluating its analgosedation safety and efficacy (3). The pharmacology of ketamine is complex, and dose-dependent: analgesic effects usually predominate at lower doses (0.1-0.4 mg/kg/hr) and sedative effects at higher doses (0.4-1.0 mg/kg/hr) (1, 2). 

The ketamine patients in our analysis who developed delirium received a median ketamine infusion dose of 0.5 mg/kg/hr-a dose similar to that reported in other ketamine analgosedation studies (9,11,12). The undesirable psychiatric symptoms of ketamine including psychosis and hallucinations are most common at doses greater than or equal to 1 mg/kg/hr (7).

Title: Exploring Ketamine Analgosedation Use and Its Effect on Incident Delirium in Critically Ill Adults
Snippet: Our study has important strengths. We evaluated close to 1,000 adults who were critically ill (median APACHE-IV score = 67), prospectively collected data on both ketamine use and common delirium risk variables, rigorously evaluated both delirium and coma tid, and ensured patients with delirium prior to ketamine initiation were excluded. We then evaluated the risk of ketamine for incident delirium in a regression model that accounted for delirium risk variables that were different between the delirium and nondelirium groups (4). 

Our study also has limitations. The number of patients in our cohort who received ketamine was low; ketamine analgosedation is most often used in patients with high sedative needs. The wide CIs that surround the odds ratios for delirium risk we present weaken the precision of our findings. A consistent approach for ketamine analgosedation prescribing was not in place throughout the study; the specific prescribing rationale for ketamine initiation and titration was not known. The high proportion of ketamine patients who developed incident delirium precluded determining whether the ketamine dose or infusion duration affects this risk. Delirium risk factors not included in our analysis may have affected our results. For patients having delirium prior to or on the same day of ketamine initiation, the contributory effect of ketamine to delirium occurrence remains unknown. 

We were not able to consider whether the time from ICU admission to ketamine initiation affects delirium risk. The results of our single-hospital analysis may be different in ICUs where ketamine prescribing practices are different, patients have different delirium risks, or delirium prevention and treatment strategies are different or unavailable (e.g., IV clonidine). Some of the delirium treatment strategies may have been used for nondelirium treatment indications (e.g., haloperidol for postoperative nausea and vomiting). We did not collect data on daily ABCDEF bundle use.

Title: Exploring Ketamine Analgosedation Use and Its Effect on Incident Delirium in Critically Ill Adults
Snippet: The undesirable psychiatric symptoms of ketamine including psychosis and hallucinations are most common at doses greater than or equal to 1 mg/kg/hr (7). 

The lower frequency of delirium reported in the ketamine group of Perbert et al's (11) trial compared to our results may be due to the fact ketamine was administered as a fixed-dose infusion 2.5 times lower in their trial than the average dose administered to the patients in our study who developed delirium. The results of our prospective cohort analysis are challenging compared with retrospective, cohort studies where the rigor of delirium assessment was unclear and important ICU risk factors for delirium including daily severity of illness, coma occurrence, and opioid and benzodiazepine exposure were not considered (1,2,(8)(9)(10). 

The reason(s) for the very high prevalence of incident delirium we report in the ketamine-exposed patents in  our cohort remains unclear. We carefully considered common ICU delirium risk factors and compared delirium characteristics, treatments, and outcomes between the ketamine and no-ketamine patients who developed ICU incident delirium. Although more ketamine-treated patients received opioid therapy prior to delirium, ICU opioid exposure prior to delirium occurrence was included as a variable in our regression model. Although we were not able to evaluate all delirium symptoms, some of which may be directly related to the known clinical response to ketamine therapy (e.g., hallucinations), the motoric subtypes of delirium we report and use of treatments for delirium including restraints, antipsychotics, and dexmedetomidine were similar. Although data on the occurrence of severe agitation were not able to be collected, the use of sedatives (including IV clonidine and IV haloperidol) and restraints was similar between the ketamine and nonketamine delirium groups. 

Our study has important strengths.

Title: Exploring Ketamine Analgosedation Use and Its Effect on Incident Delirium in Critically Ill Adults
Snippet: In conclusion, our study suggests ketamine analgosedation in critically ill surgical and medical adults may contribute to an increased risk for incident ICU delirium. Despite the extensive comparative analyses conducted between the ketamine and nonketamine groups who developed delirium, the mechanisms for delirium in patients receiving ketamine analgesedation remain unclear. Future, well-designed, prospective, randomized trials are needed to carefully evaluate the magnitude of delirium risk associated ketamine analgosedation and whether psychiatric symptoms observed during ketamine therapy truly represent delirium.

Title: Exploring Ketamine Analgosedation Use and Its Effect on Incident Delirium in Critically Ill Adults
Snippet: K etamine, an anesthetic with both analgesic and sedative properties, is increasingly being used in both surgical and medical critically ill adults for analgosedation (1)(2)(3). Delirium, a common sequela of critical illness, is associated with poor outcomes (4). Medications, including benzodiazepines (5) and opioids (6), are well-established risk factors for delirium in the ICU. Ketamine, an N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor antagonist, results in a dissociative state clinically manifesting as catatonia and amnesia, and is associated in a dose-dependent fashion with hallucinations and psychosis (7). Similarities exist between the clinical effects of ketamine and the symptoms of delirium (4). 

One randomized trial (8) and four cohort studies (9)(10)(11)(12) have evaluated delirium in critically ill adults managed with ketamine analogosedation. In the randomized trial (8), the ketamine dose administered was low and fixed, and compared with the placebo group, the ketamine group received fewer opioids, an important dose-related risk for delirium (6). None of the ICU cohort studies reported a difference in delirium with ketamine use (9)(10)(11)(12). However, none of these studies considered the presence of other potential baseline and ICU delirium risk factors nor ensured delirium occurred after ketamine was started. The risk for ICU delirium with ketamine analgosedation and the characteristics and outcomes of delirium that occur after its initiation remain poorly characterized. We compared variables, including ketamine analgosedation use, between critically ill adults who developed ICU incident delirium and those who did not, evaluated whether ketamine analgosedation increases delirium risk, and compared delirium characteristics, treatments, and outcomes between ketamine and nonketamine patients who developed delirium.

Although more ketamine-treated patients received opioid therapy prior to delirium, ICU opioid exposure prior to delirium occurrence was included as a variable in our regression model. Although we were not able to evaluate all delirium symptoms, some of which may be directly related to the known clinical response to ketamine therapy (e.g., hallucinations), the motoric subtypes of delirium we report and use of treatments for delirium including restraints, antipsychotics, and dexmedetomidine were similar. Although data on the occurrence of severe agitation were not able to be collected, the use of sedatives (including IV clonidine and IV haloperidol) and restraints was similar between the ketamine and nonketamine delirium groups. 

Our study has important strengths.

documents.title: Exploring Ketamine Analgosedation Use and Its Effect on Incident Delirium in Critically Ill Adults
documents.snippet: In conclusion, our study suggests ketamine analgosedation in critically ill surgical and medical adults may contribute to an increased risk for incident ICU delirium. Despite the extensive comparative analyses conducted between the ketamine and nonketamine groups who developed delirium, the mechanisms for delirium in patients receiving ketamine analgesedation remain unclear. Future, well-designed, prospective, randomized trials are needed to carefully evaluate the magnitude of delirium risk associated ketamine analgosedation and whether psychiatric symptoms observed during ketamine therapy truly represent delirium.

documents.title: Exploring Ketamine Analgosedation Use and Its Effect on Incident Delirium in Critically Ill Adults
documents.snippet:
K etamine, an anesthetic with both analgesic and sedative properties, is increasingly being used in both surgical and medical critically ill adults for analgosedation (1)(2)(3). Delirium, a common sequela of critical illness, is associated with poor outcomes (4). Medications, including benzodiazepines (5) and opioids (6), are well-established risk factors for delirium in the ICU. Ketamine, an N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor antagonist, results in a dissociative state clinically manifesting as catatonia and amnesia, and is associated in a dose-dependent fashion with hallucinations and psychosis (7). Similarities exist between the clinical effects of ketamine and the symptoms of delirium (4). 

One randomized trial (8) and four cohort studies (9)(10)(11)(12) have evaluated delirium in critically ill adults managed with ketamine analogosedation. In the randomized trial (8), the ketamine dose administered was low and fixed, and compared with the placebo group, the ketamine group received fewer opioids, an important dose-related risk for delirium (6). None of the ICU cohort studies reported a difference in delirium with ketamine use (9)(10)(11)(12). However, none of these studies considered the presence of other potential baseline and ICU delirium risk factors nor ensured delirium occurred after ketamine was started. The risk for ICU delirium with ketamine analgosedation and the characteristics and outcomes of delirium that occur after its initiation remain poorly characterized. We compared variables, including ketamine analgosedation use, between critically ill adults who developed ICU incident delirium and those who did not, evaluated whether ketamine analgosedation increases delirium risk, and compared delirium characteristics, treatments, and outcomes between ketamine and nonketamine patients who developed delirium.

Title: Does haloperidol prophylaxis reduce ketamine-induced emergence delirium in children?
Snippet: OBJECTIVES
Ketamine is a non-barbiturate agent with rapid action onset that induces profound sedation; however, some emergency physicians tend not to use ketamine because of the risk of emergence delirium (ED). This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of haloperidol prophylaxis in postoperative ketamine delirium in children.


METHODS
Prospective data relating to any emergence dreams, delirium, hallucinations, agitation, crying, altered perceptions, and necessary interventions were recorded in consecutive cases of ketamine delirium in patients attending Mansoura University Hospital, Egypt, from June 2010 to May 2011.


RESULTS
A total of 537 records were available for analysis. Of those, 267 received prophylactic haloperidol (49.7%). There were significant differences between the two groups regarding post-anaesthetic care unit behaviour. The ketamine-haloperidol groups included more patients who were sleepy, calm (P ≤0.01) and less irritable (P ≤0.01), with a lower incidence of crying (P ≤0.01) and disorientation (P ≤0.01).


CONCLUSION
We found that preoperative administration of haloperidol decreases the incidence of postoperative delirium in a sample of Egyptian children undergoing minor surgery. This is congruent with earlier work conducted in adults. This work carries great hope to decrease and even prevent ED in hospitalised, non-surgical patients.

Title: Caudal block and emergence delirium in pediatric patients: Is it analgesia or sedation?
Snippet: Background: Emergence delirium (ED) although a short-lived and self-limiting phenomenon, makes a child prone to injury in the immediate postoperative period and hence is a cause of concern not only to the pediatric anesthesiologist, surgeons, and post anesthesia care unit staff but also amongst parents. Additional medication to quieten the child offsets the potential benefits of rapid emergence and delays recovery in day care settings. There is conflicting evidence of influence of analgesia and sedation following anesthesia on emergence agitation. We hypothesized that an anesthetic technique which improves analgesia and prolongs emergence time will reduce the incidence of ED. We selected ketamine as adjuvant to caudal block for this purpose. Methods: This randomized, double blind prospective study was performed in 150 premedicated children ASA I, II, aged 2 to 8 years who were randomly assigned to either group B (caudal with bupivacaine), BK (bupivacaine and ketamine), or NC (no caudal), soon after LMA placement. Recovery characteristics and complications were recorded. Results: Emergence time, duration of pain relief, and Pediatric Anesthesia Emergence Delirium (PAED) scores were significantly higher in the NC group (P<0.05). Duration of analgesia and emergence time were significantly more in group BK than groups B and NC. However, the discharge readiness was comparable between all groups. No patient in BK group required to be given any medication to treat ED. Conclusion: Emergence time as well as duration of analgesia have significant influence on incidence of emergence delirium. Ketamine, as caudal adjuvant is a promising agent to protect against ED in children, following sevoflurane anesthesia.

Snippet: With the reduction of pain, our study demonstrated a lower 30-day readmission rate with the administration of intraoperative ketamine, which may be due to the reduction in post-operative pain. Additionally, due to the incidence of opioid-induced delirium, transitioning post-operative pain regimens to include ketamine has been thought to reduce the incidence of opioidinduced delirium (8). In fact, in a small prospective cohort of 58 patients, Hudetz and colleagues demonstrated a 30% reduction in postoperative delirium after cardiac surgery with perioperative ketamine administration (25). However, the administration of intraoperative ketamine is decided by the providing surgical team on an individual basis. 

While many post-operative pain regimens across surgical specialties have since transitioned to include ketamine, there is a paucity of evidence attributing delirium-protectant effects of ketamine (8). In a systematic literature review of the association between "ketamine" and "postoperative delirium", Avidan et al. yielded six studies with two demonstrating decreased delirium, one with an increase in delirium, one with equivocal results, and two without any delirium patients (8). As a result of inconsistent findings throughout the literature, Avidan and colleagues conducted an international, multicenter, double-blind, randomized clinical trial with 672 elderly patients (≥60 years old) undergoing major surgeries (8). The authors concluded that there were no significant differences in the incidence postoperative delirium, postoperative pain, or postoperative opioid usage between the ketamine and control groups (8). 

In fact, the authors found that patients receiving ketamine tended to have an increased incidence of hallucinations and nightmares (8). This particular finding has been noted previously (5) and is also formally in the American Pain Association's guidelines for consideration. Ketamine is an NMDA and HCN1 antagonist that lead to dissociative anesthesia that includes hypnosis and analgesia (26).

Snippet: In a study conducted by Kain et al on preoperative anxiety and emergence delirium and postoperative maladaptive behaviors, it was found that the odds having marked symptoms of emergence delirium increased by 10% for each increment of 10 points in the child's state anxiety score. [12] It was a limiting factor in our study as it directly affected the study parameter. 

Some other limiting factors in the study include the stark inability to distinguish between emergence agitation and postoperative pain because of their similar presentation in pediatric patients and the absence of a standardized method of analyzing the incidence and severity of emergence agitation which may lead to discrepancies in the results of various conducted studies. 

In conclusion, intravenous ketamine is more effective than intravenous midazolam in decreasing the incidence and severity of emergence agitation in pediatric patients undergoing general anesthesia with sevoflurane. Premedication with ketamine was also associated with decreased requirement of rescue analgesia and an earlier discharge from PACU thus rendering it a better choice for pediatric patients undergoing surgeries under general anesthesia.

Title: Comparison of Ketamine to Haloperidol for Preventing Delirium in ICU Elderly Patients
Snippet: There were no significant differences in the delirium incidence between the ketamine groups and the placebo group, and neither the low dose (0.5 mg/kg) nor the high dose (1 mg/kg) of ketamine reduced the incidence of delirium in patients over 60 years of age (34). 

Disturbance in the synthesis and release of neurotransmitters, such as reduced cholinergic and serotonergic activity and excess release of glutamate, can lead to functional connectivity alteration of neurons, resulting in atrophy and brain damage, which play crucial roles in delirium development (47)(48)(49)(50)(51). Ketamine has been shown to balance these neurotransmitter releases in the brain (52)(53)(54). Moreover, the beneficial effect of ketamine on preventing delirium might be due to its anti-inflammatory properties (27), neuroprotective activity (55), and anti-depressant properties (56). A study by Hudetz et al. on elderly patients undergoing cardiac surgery showed that the injection of 0.5 mg/kg of ketamine during the anesthesia decreased the incidence of postoperative delirium. The reduction in delirium was associated with a decrease in serum C-reactive protein (CRP) concentrations, suggesting the anti-inflammatory function of ketamine (29). 

Inflammation plays a significant role in the development of delirium, as indicated by previous studies (57,58). Surgical trauma, for instance, can trigger an elevation in inflammatory markers, such as CRP, which can subsequently promote the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). These ROS have the potential to induce disruption of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and contribute to the onset of delirium (57). Ketamine's anti-inflammatory properties might contribute to its potential in reducing delirium through several mechanisms.

Title: Delirium pattern in hospitalized patients of a tertiary care rural hospital: An observational study
Snippet: As such, a thorough understanding of the various factors and types is critical for effective diagnosis and treatment of delirium. 

Current literature sug gests that delirium results from complex neurobiological processes, including neurotransmitter imbalances, inflammatory responses, and oxidative stress. For example, disruptions in cholinergic and dopaminergic neurotransmission are commonly implicated in delirium pathophysiology. [8] Furthermore, systemic inflammation, often secondary to infections or surgical trauma, is known to contribute to delirium onset by promoting neuroinflammation and blood-brain barrier dysfunction. [9] Metabolic disturbances such as hyponatremia and hypoxia have also been identified as significant contributors, especially in elderly patients who are more vulnerable to such changes. [10]  this scenario, the management of delirium requires a comprehensive approach that addresses both the predisposing and precipitating factors. This is particularly relevant in rural healthcare settings where challenges related to early recognition and appropriate management are compounded by limited healthcare infrastructure and expertise. [11] Thus, this study aimed to explore the etiological spectrum and motor subtypes of delirium in a rural tertiary care hospital in Central India, offering insights into its association with sociodemographic factors. Such data is essential to improve clinical practices and healthcare outcomes for delirium patients in resource-limited settings.

Title: Sleep and Delirium in Older Adults
Snippet: While delirium is a multifactorial phenomenon, with several proposed pathophysiological mechanisms, mechanistic research has been slow in part due a lack of wellestablished animal models and an absence of easily obtainable biomarkers [14]. Among the neurological pathways hypothesized to precipitate delirium, one involves the prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate, and basal ganglia, and another involves the parietal lobes, superior colliculus, and thalamic pulvinar nucleus [15]. More recently, a functional network comprised of several interconnected brain structures has been implicated in delirium [16]. Disturbances in these pathways lead to decreased cholinergic activity and dopaminergic excess, contributing to delirium [17]. # Summary
