Title: Intraoperative ketamine does not affect postoperative delirium or pain after major surgery in older adults: an international, multicentre, double-blind, randomised clinical trial
Snippet: Evidence before this study Delirium and pain are both common and serious complications of surgery. These complications cause distress to patients and family members, and are associated with worse postoperative outcomes. Opioids are the mainstay drugs to treat postoperative pain, but also cause delirium and are associated with lifethreatening complications and addiction. At present, there is no pharmacological treatment for delirium. In order to assess the effect of perioperative ketamine on postoperative delirium and pain, we did a systematic search of randomised trials and systematic reviews published in any language. We searched the following databases for studies published up to Feb 5, 2014, (the start of enrolment into the PODCAST trial): MEDLINE, PubMed, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled trials, Web of Science, metaRegister of controlled trials, LILACS, African Health-line, POPLINE, MedCarib, CINAHL, and Clinicaltrials.gov using the following search terms: "ketamine and postoperative delirium" and "ketamine and postoperative pain." The systematic search for "ketamine" and "postoperative delirium" included all randomised controlled trials with surgical patients aged 60 years or older published between 1964 (when ketamine was introduced in clinical practice) and 2014. We identified six studies with a total of 357 patients. Of the six trials, two showed a decrease in delirium with ketamine, one showed an increase in delirium, one had equivocal results, and in two trials there were no patients with delirium. In contrast to the dearth of studies examining the effect of ketamine on postoperative delirium, there have been many studies examining the effect of perioperative ketamine on postoperative pain, with ketamine administered at various doses, at different times, and for variable durations. The vast majority of these studies enrolled fewer than 100 patients, and a few enrolled up to 150 patients. A systematic review of 70 of these trials involving 4701 patients published in 2011 showed that a subanaesthetic dose of ketamine decreased pain for up to 48 h and decreased requirement for opioids after surgery.
</snippet>

Title: Comparison of Ketamine to Haloperidol for Preventing Delirium in ICU Elderly Patients
Snippet: Ketamine, an intravenous anesthetic, is increasingly being used as an alternative agent to treat symptoms of agitation and delirium (19,25,26). Emerging preclinical and clinical research has shown the neuroprotective properties of ketamine (27). A small clinical trial involving cardiac surgery patients showed that administering a low dose of ketamine significantly reduced postoperative delirium without causing any noticeable side effects (28). Moreover, the administration of low-dose ketamine was shown to improve postoperative cognitive impairment following cardiac surgery (29). Furthermore, ketamine has been found to reduce the incidence of emergency delirium in children (30). Ketamine is a safe, fast-acting, and effective treatment for reducing delirium, possibly due to its neuroprotective effects (31). Additionally, ketamine is cost-effective and has been extensively utilized by anesthetists for over six decades. Although there is growing evidence supporting the use of ketamine in delirium prevention, studies are limited, and the current research has not definitively established its efficacy in older hospitalized patients (32). 

There are few studies investigating the efficacy of ketamine as a first-line treatment for elderly patients with delirium (33,34). The present study aimed to investigate the safety and efficacy of administering low-dose ketamine as a potential treatment for reducing delirium in elderly ICU patients. The current study hypothesized that the use of ketamine would be effective in controlling delirium symptoms when compared to the commonly used medication haloperidol. By conducting a randomized clinical trial, this study sought to evaluate the hypothesis and provide insights into the potential benefits of ketamine as a first-line treatment for delirium in elderly patients.
</snippet>

Title: Therapeutic potential of ketamine in management of epilepsy: Clinical implications and mechanistic insights.
Snippet: Epilepsy, a widespread neurological disorder, affects approximately 50 million people worldwide. This disorder is typified by recurring seizures due to abnormal neuron communication in the brain. The seizures can lead to severe ischemia and hypoxia, potentially threatening patients' lives. However, with proper diagnosis and treatment, up to 70 % of patients can live without seizures. The causes of epilepsy are complex and multifactorial, encompassing genetic abnormalities, structural brain anomalies, ion channel dysfunctions, neurotransmitter imbalances, neuroinflammation, and immune system involvement. These factors collectively disrupt the crucial balance between excitation and inhibition within the brain, leading to epileptic seizures. The management of treatment-resistant epilepsy remains a considerable challenge, necessitating innovative therapeutic approaches. Among emerging potential treatments, ketamine-a drug traditionally employed for anesthesia and depression-has demonstrated efficacy in reducing seizures. It is noteworthy that, independent of its anti-epileptic effects, ketamine has been found to improve the balance between excitatory and inhibitory (E/I) activities in the brain. The balance is crucial for maintaining normal neural function, and its disruption is widely considered a key driver of epileptic seizures. By acting on N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors and other potential mechanisms, ketamine may regulate neuronal excitability, reduce excessive synchronized neural activity, and counteract epileptic seizures. This positive impact on E/I balance reinforces the potential of ketamine as a promising drug for treating epilepsy, especially in patients who are insensitive to traditional anti-epileptic drugs. This review aims to consolidate the current understanding of ketamine's therapeutic role in epilepsy. It will focus its impact on neuronal excitability and synaptic plasticity, its neuroprotective qualities, and elucidate the drug's potential mechanisms of action in treating epilepsy. By scrutinizing ketamine's impact and mechanisms in various types of epilepsy, we aspire to contribute to a more comprehensive and holistic approach to epilepsy management.
</snippet>

Title: Ketamine can produce oscillatory dynamics by engaging mechanisms dependent on the kinetics of NMDA receptors
Snippet: In our work, we showed how NMDA R antagonism in a simple cortical network can give rise to gamma and slow-delta oscillations. However, ketamine can have molecular effects other than NMDA R antagonism. Furthermore, systemic administration of ketamine will affect all structures in the central nervous system. 

The interaction between the cortex, the thalamus and the brainstem can contribute to slow-delta oscillatory dynamics. Indeed, removing significant excitatory input from the brainstem to the cortex can result in slow-delta oscillations [35]. Ketamine can also decrease the activity in excitatory arousal pathways from the parabrachial nucleus and the medial pontine reticular formation in the brainstem to the thalamus and basal forebrain through NMDA R antagonism [36]. The coordination of down-states observed between cortex and thalamus suggests a mechanistic coordination between these two structures [16]. All of these indicate that other slow-delta oscillatory mechanisms can come into play to enhance or complement the mechanisms mediated by NMDA R antagonism at the cortical level. 

Ketamine can also alter hyperpolarization-activated nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels [18] for slowdelta oscillatory contributions. In fact, low doses of ketamine have been found to produce 3 Hz oscillations in posteromedial cortex [3,12]. These 3 Hz oscillations have been found to rely on HCN channels [3]. Ketamine may act on these channels either indirectly through NMDA R antagonism [3] or directly by inhibiting them [18] to produce these oscillations. Again, these mechanisms can enhance or complement the mechanisms mediated by NMDA R antagonism at the cortical level.
</snippet>

Title: Ketamine can produce oscillatory dynamics by engaging mechanisms dependent on the kinetics of NMDA receptors
Snippet: To examine these mechanisms, we developed a biophysical model of a cortical network exposed to ketamine. When we introduce ketamine as an NMDA R antagonist, our model replicates the brain dynamics in human subjects and non-human primates administered ketamine and reveals brain mechanisms underlying the generation of these dynamics. Our model incorporates detailed kinetics for NMDA R dynamics that underlie these mechanisms. By dissecting the model through simulations, we report three advances. 

First, we have established that NMDA R antagonism under ketamine can terminate spiking in active neurons with subthreshold background excitation. We find that, even when NMDA R s are antagonized non-preferentially across all neurons, global disinhibition can emerge when tonic inhibition is provided by interneurons with subthreshold background excitation or high resting membrane potential. Second, we have discovered an NMDA R -dependent mechanism that can generate gamma oscillations in a cortical network, through an interaction between NMDA-and GABA-receptor-mediated currents. As NMDA R closing is known to be slow, this mechanisms stands in contrast to established mechanisms for gamma generation that rely on fast AMPA-and GABA-receptor transmission, such as the pyramidal-interneuronal gamma mechanism [13]. Third, we have discovered an NMDA R -dependent mechanism that can generate slow-delta oscillations in a cortical network, also through an interaction between NMDA-and GABA-receptor-mediated currents. This mechanism relies on an imbalance between excitatory and inhibitory activity, and stands in contrast to established mechanisms for slow-delta generation that rely on membrane channels, such as sodium-activated [14] and ATP-activated [15] potassium channels. 

Through these findings, we explain how the effects of ketamine extend from the subcellular level to the network level to produce the oscillatory dynamics observed in brain activity. Our work proposes new general mechanisms for generating brain dynamics, provides new insight into the mechanism of action of ketamine, and suggests new mechanisms by which ketamine can provide therapeutic effects that go beyond anesthesia, dissociation and analgesia.

Title: The impact of ketamine on outcomes in critically ill patients: a systematic review with meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis of randomized controlled trials
Snippet: In this work, we evaluated the effect of ketamine in critically ill ICU patients. Our meta-analysis of 12 RCTs did not demonstrate differences between ketamine and control groups regarding mortality, pain intensity, opioid or midazolam consumption, and ICU LOS. However, ketamine reduced the delirium rate. This result is significant but may not be robust, and additional RCTs should be conducted in the future. The result on incidences of delirium was sensitive to exclusion of three of four studies, in which case the model showed no difference between the groups. The result on mean opioid consumption was sensitive to exclusion of either one of two studies. For all other outcomes, the result was not sensitive to exclusion of any study. Title: Recent Advances in Preventing and Managing Postoperative Delirium
Snippet: Ketamine has been found to reduce postoperative inflammation 32 , improve perioperative pain outcomes 33 , and reduce excitotoxicity in laboratory models 34 . Results from a small trial also demonstrated decreased occurrence of delirium and decreased incidence of delayed neurocognitive recovery in cardiac surgery patients who received intraoperative ketamine compared with placebo 35,36 . With this background and rationale, an international team of investigators conducted the PODCAST (Prevention of Delirium and Complications Associated with Surgical Treatments) trial, hypothesizing that a sub-anesthetic, intraoperative dose of ketamine would reduce postoperative delirium 37 . In this trial, ketamine had no statistically significant effect on delirium incidence (ketamine groups: 19.45%, placebo group: 19.82%, absolute difference 0.36%, 95% confidence interval [CI] −6.07 to 7.38; P = 0.92), delirium severity, or delirium recurrence 2 . Instead, dose-dependent increases were reported for postoperative hallucinations (18% in the placebo group, 20% in the 0.5 mg/kg ketamine group, and 28% in the 1.0 mg/kg ketamine group; P = 0.01) and nightmares (8% in the placebo group, 12% in the 0.5 mg/kg ketamine group, and 15% in the 1.0 mg/kg ketamine group; P = 0.03). These findings align with previously known psychoactive side effects of ketamine 33,38,39 . Thus, intraoperative ketamine probably does not prevent delirium; rather, ketamine may increase the risk of adverse perioperative psychoactive experiences. 

Dexmedetomidine has also been tested in large randomized trials in relation to postoperative delirium. A 2014 meta-analysis examined dexmedetomidine use across 14 trials involving cardiac surgery and intensive care unit (ICU) patients 40 .
</snippet>

Title: Intraoperative ketamine does not affect postoperative delirium or pain after major surgery in older adults: an international, multicentre, double-blind, randomised clinical trial
Snippet: Evidence before this study Delirium and pain are both common and serious complications of surgery. These complications cause distress to patients and family members, and are associated with worse postoperative outcomes. Opioids are the mainstay drugs to treat postoperative pain, but also cause delirium and are associated with lifethreatening complications and addiction. At present, there is no pharmacological treatment for delirium. In order to assess the effect of perioperative ketamine on postoperative delirium and pain, we did a systematic search of randomised trials and systematic reviews published in any language. We searched the following databases for studies published up to Feb 5, 2014, (the start of enrolment into the PODCAST trial): MEDLINE, PubMed, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled trials, Web of Science, metaRegister of controlled trials, LILACS, African Health-line, POPLINE, MedCarib, CINAHL, and Clinicaltrials.gov using the following search terms: "ketamine and postoperative delirium" and "ketamine and postoperative pain." The systematic search for "ketamine" and "postoperative delirium" included all randomised controlled trials with surgical patients aged 60 years or older published between 1964 (when ketamine was introduced in clinical practice) and 2014. We identified six studies with a total of 357 patients. Of the six trials, two showed a decrease in delirium with ketamine, one showed an increase in delirium, one had equivocal results, and in two trials there were no patients with delirium. In contrast to the dearth of studies examining the effect of ketamine on postoperative delirium, there have been many studies examining the effect of perioperative ketamine on postoperative pain, with ketamine administered at various doses, at different times, and for variable durations. The vast majority of these studies enrolled fewer than 100 patients, and a few enrolled up to 150 patients. A systematic review of 70 of these trials involving 4701 patients published in 2011 showed that a subanaesthetic dose of ketamine decreased pain for up to 48 h and decreased requirement for opioids after surgery.

Title: Perioperative ketamine administration to prevent delirium and neurocognitive disorders after surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Snippet: Background: Surgery induces high rates of cognitive disorders, persisting for up to 12 months in elderly adults. This review aimed to assess the currently debated preventive effect of perioperative ketamine on postoperative delirium and postoperative neurocognitive disorders (POND). Materials and methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis including all randomized controlled trials investigating the effects of perioperative ketamine administration in adult patients compared to placebo or no intervention on postoperative delirium and/or POND between January 2007 and April 2022. Database searches were conducted in PubMed, Medline, Embase, Scopus, and Central. Random effects models were used to pool overall estimates. The GRADE approach was used to assess the quality of the evidence. Results: From 1379 records screened, 14 randomized controlled trials with 1618 patients randomized met our inclusion criteria with a high level of consensus among reviewers, amongst whom 50% were at low-moderate risk of bias. There was no between-group difference in postoperative delirium [8 trials, 1265 patients, odds ratio (OR) 0.93, 95% CI (0.51–1.70), I 2=28%] and POND [5 trials, 494 patients, OR 0.52, 95% CI (0.15–1.80); I 2=78%]. There was no significant between-group difference in postoperative psychological adverse effects, level of pain, hospital length of stay, or mortality. Between-group subgroup analyses showed no difference in delirium or POND incidence according to surgical setting, ketamine dose, mode of administration, combination or not with other drug(s), and assessment timing or definition of cognitive disorders. Conclusion: Perioperative ketamine does not prevent postoperative delirium or POND. Significant study heterogeneity suggests that standardized measures for POND assessment and a specific focus on patients at high risk for POND should be used to improve the comparability of future studies.

# Summary

Ketamine reduces delirium incidence in selected clinical settings primarily through N‑methyl‑D‑aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonism that rebalances cortical excitation–inhibition dynamics, dampens excessive synchronous neural activity, and may limit perioperative neuroinflammation and excitotoxic stress; however, clinical benefits are heterogeneous across trials, and psychoactive adverse effects can occur, especially at higher subanesthetic doses. <cite id="a77aeeb8-0">Across perioperative randomized trials, ketamine consistently decreases postoperative pain and opioid exposure but yields mixed effects on delirium—some trials show reductions, others increases or equivocal results—with no patients with delirium in a few small studies</cite> <cite id="559b9c4b-0">Ketamine’s antiseizure effects arise from restoring the excitation–inhibition balance, an imbalance that underlies seizures and contributes to brain dysfunction</cite> <cite id="559b9c4b-1">NMDA antagonism preferentially affects GABAergic interneurons, disinhibiting pyramidal neurons, elevating extracellular glutamate, and increasing gamma activity acutely, with chronic exposure shifting toward cortical hypoactivity; these mechanisms link to both plasticity and potential excitotoxicity</cite> <cite id="559b9c4b-3">At the network level, NMDA antagonism can generate gamma and slow‑delta oscillations and alter thalamocortical and brainstem arousal pathways, suggesting multi‑site mechanisms relevant to arousal and confusion states</cite> <cite id="2efb7124-0">A meta‑analysis of 12 ICU RCTs found ketamine reduced delirium rates overall but the effect was sensitive to exclusion of a few studies and should be interpreted cautiously</cite> <cite id="2efb7124-1">In the large PODCAST trial, subanesthetic intraoperative ketamine did not reduce delirium but increased hallucinations and nightmares in a dose‑dependent fashion, aligning with known psychoactive side effects</cite> <cite id="2efb7124-4">A more recent meta‑analysis of 14 perioperative RCTs (2007–2022) similarly found no difference in delirium (OR 0.93) and suggested perioperative ketamine does not prevent delirium or POND overall, with substantial heterogeneity and no clear dose/formulation/subgroup advantage for delirium</cite>.

# Mechanistic rationale: NMDA antagonism and delirium biology

Delirium involves acute disturbances of attention and cognition linked to neuroinflammation, excitatory–inhibitory imbalance, and abnormal cortical and thalamic oscillations. <cite id="559b9c4b-0">Ketamine reduces seizures in experimental models by restoring E/I balance, an effect attributed to NMDA receptor blockade and downstream regulation of neuronal excitability and synaptic plasticity</cite>. <cite id="559b9c4b-1">By preferentially inhibiting NMDA receptors on GABAergic interneurons—especially parvalbumin‑positive cells—ketamine transiently disinhibits cortical pyramidal neurons, elevates extracellular glutamate, and increases gamma oscillations; chronic or high‑load exposure shifts toward alpha‑band cortical slowing and interneuron dysfunction, reflecting a biphasic trajectory from hyperexcitability to hypoexcitability</cite>. <cite id="559b9c4b-3">Computational and experimental work shows NMDA antagonism can terminate spiking under subthreshold background excitation, generate NMDA‑dependent gamma oscillations via interplay with GABAergic currents, and produce slow‑delta dynamics through E/I imbalance; ketamine also reduces activity in brainstem arousal pathways and can engage HCN channels, thereby modulating thalamocortical synchronization</cite>. <cite id="559b9c4b-2">NMDA antagonism can potentiate anticonvulsant effects when combined with other agents in seizure models, supporting the broader anticonvulsant profile of NMDA blockade</cite>. Collectively, these mechanisms suggest that ketamine’s NMDA antagonism can stabilize cortical networks, reduce excessive synchronous activity associated with delirium, and potentially mitigate neuroinflammation and excitotoxic cascades that contribute to acute cognitive decompensation during perioperative stressors. <cite id="559b9c4b-1">Acute glutamate surges and gamma increases may support adaptive plasticity, whereas prolonged disinhibition risks calcium overload, mitochondrial dysfunction, and apoptosis—explaining why dosing and duration critically modulate risk/benefit</cite>.

# Clinical evidence across settings

Perioperative/ICU settings:
- Meta‑analysis in critically ill adults: <cite id="2efb7124-0">Across 12 RCTs, ketamine did not change mortality, pain intensity, opioid or midazolam use, or ICU length of stay, but reduced delirium incidence overall; sensitivity analyses showed the delirium difference disappeared when three of four studies were excluded, and opioid effects were sensitive to one study, warranting cautious interpretation</cite>. 
- Large randomized trial (PODCAST): <cite id="2efb7124-1">In older adults undergoing major surgery, subanesthetic intraoperative ketamine did not reduce delirium incidence (19.45% vs 19.82%), severity, or recurrence; higher ketamine doses were associated with increased postoperative hallucinations (20% at 0.5 mg/kg; 28% at 1.0 mg/kg) and nightmares</cite>.
- Updated perioperative meta‑analysis (2007–2022): <cite id="2efb7124-4">No preventive effect on delirium (OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.51–1.70) or POND (OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.15–1.80), with significant heterogeneity and no differences by surgical setting, dose, route, combination therapy, timing, or cognitive outcome definitions; authors concluded perioperative ketamine does not prevent delirium/POND overall</cite>. 
- Historical synthesis: <cite id="a77aeeb8-0">Earlier perioperative literature up to 2014 identified six RCTs in older surgical patients: two showed decreased delirium with ketamine, one an increase, one equivocal, and two with no delirium; ketamine consistently reduced pain and opioid need</cite>.

Cardiac surgery:
- Small randomized trials reported benefits: <cite id="a77aeeb8-1">A small cardiac surgery trial found a low dose of intraoperative ketamine significantly reduced postoperative delirium without notable side effects and improved postoperative cognitive impairment in follow‑up</cite>. 
- In PODCAST’s cardiac surgery cohort, however, no delirium prevention was observed and psychoactive adverse effects rose with dose. <cite id="2efb7124-1">These divergent results highlight heterogeneity in protocols, dosing, population, and assessment methods</cite>.

Neurosurgery and pediatric emergency:
- Neuroprotection and reduced seizures may indirectly lower delirium risk in neurosurgical ICU contexts: <cite id="559b9c4b-0">Ketamine improves E/I balance and reduces seizures in epilepsy models, supporting neuroprotection under hypoxia/ischemia</cite> <cite id="559b9c4b-1">NMDA antagonism’s interneuron‑specific effects and oscillatory mechanisms map to cortical hyperexcitability relevant to neurosurgical injury</cite>. 
- Pediatric emergency care: <cite id="a77aeeb8-1">Ketamine reduced emergency delirium incidence in children and is used to treat agitation/delirium with rapid onset and efficacy, possibly due to neuroprotective and psychoactive properties</cite>.

Opioid‑sparing and analgesia‑driven pathways:
- Analgesic and sedation sparing are consistent: <cite id="a77aeeb8-0">Subanesthetic ketamine decreases postoperative pain and opioid requirements for up to 48 hours; opioids themselves increase delirium risk via cognitive side effects</cite>. 
- Mechanistically, <cite id="2efb7124-1">ketamine’s anti‑inflammatory and anti‑excitotoxic effects, along with improved pain control, provide plausible downstream benefits on delirium, even when direct prevention is not demonstrated in large RCTs</cite>. 

# How NMDA antagonism translates to lower delirium risk

Direct and indirect mechanisms have been proposed:
- Restoring E/I balance: <cite id="559b9c4b-0">By antagonizing NMDA receptors, ketamine reduces excessive neuronal hyperexcitability that contributes to seizures and cortical dysfunction during perioperative stress</cite>, thereby stabilizing arousal and attention networks. 
- Network oscillations and thalamocortical control: <cite id="559b9c4b-3">Ketamine’s NMDA antagonism terminates spiking under subthreshold excitation, generates NMDA‑dependent gamma oscillations, and reduces activity in brainstem arousal pathways to the thalamus/basal forebrain</cite>, mechanisms that can normalize dysrhythmic cortical activity associated with delirium. 
- Neuroinflammation/excitotoxicity modulation: <cite id="559b9c4b-1">Acute NMDA blockade elevates glutamate and gamma activity via disinhibition, whereas chronic or sustained effects risk calcium overload and apoptosis; this biphasic risk profile implies that brief, low‑dose exposure may limit neuroinflammation and excitotoxic cascades without triggering persistent sedation</cite>. 

These pathways may explain why some perioperative trials report reduced delirium—especially when ketamine is integrated with multimodal strategies that minimize opioids and manage agitation—but effects are inconsistent across populations and protocols. <cite id="2efb7124-4">A recent perioperative meta‑analysis found no overall preventive effect on delirium, with substantial heterogeneity and no clear dose/formulation/subgroup advantage</cite>.

# Dosing, regimens, and the role of concomitant agents

Trials diverge in dosing and combination therapy:
- PODCAST used subanesthetic intraoperative doses (0.5–1.0 mg/kg) and found no delirium prevention with dose‑related increases in hallucinations and nightmares. <cite id="2efb7124-1">This aligns with ketamine’s known psychoactive side effects at higher subanesthetic exposures</cite>. 
- Earlier small cardiac surgery trials used low doses without notable side effects and suggested cognitive benefits; <cite id="a77aeeb8-1">heterogeneity in dosing schedules, patient selection, and assessment tools likely explains inconsistent findings</cite>. 
- Maintenance sedation and rescue pharmacology matter: <cite id="a77aeeb8-1">In ICU agitation/delirium, ketamine is compared with antipsychotics such as haloperidol; small RCTs motivate testing low‑dose ketamine as first‑line therapy due to rapid onset and efficacy, but broader evidence remains limited</cite>. 
- In ICU-wide meta-analysis, <cite id="2efb7124-0">benefits on delirium were sensitive to inclusion of specific trials, and routine analgesic/sedative protocols may modulate observed effects</cite>.

# Clinical implications across settings

ICU/general surgical:
- Overall, perioperative ketamine does not consistently prevent delirium across diverse ICU/surgical settings, but may lower rates in some protocols; risks include increased psychoactive effects. <cite id="2efb7124-4">No pooled reduction in delirium overall, with high heterogeneity and no clear moderator improving delirium outcomes</cite> <cite id="2efb7124-0">ICU meta‑analysis suggests a delirium reduction that weakens without specific RCTs</cite> <cite id="2efb7124-1">PODCAST shows no delirium prevention and dose‑related psychoactive adverse effects</cite>. 
- Practical approach: <cite id="a77aeeb8-0">Use low-dose, time-limited ketamine to minimize opioid exposure while monitoring for hallucinations and nightmares</cite>; integrate nonpharmacologic delirium prevention.

Cardiac and neurosurgical:
- Cardiac surgery: early small RCTs favor benefit and cognitive preservation, but large multi-center trials negate this; protocol details and concomitant benzodiazepines likely matter. <cite id="a77aeeb8-1">Low-dose ketamine reduced delirium with no notable side effects in a small cardiac surgery trial and improved cognitive outcomes</cite> <cite id="2efb7124-1">PODCAST showed no delirium reduction and increased hallucinations</cite>. 
- Neurosurgery/pediatrics: <cite id="559b9c4b-0">E/I restoration and antiseizure effects support potential delirium risk reduction after brain injury</cite>; <cite id="a77aeeb8-1">children’s emergency delirium decreased with ketamine</cite>. 
- Mechanistically, <cite id="559b9c4b-1">ketamine’s preferential effect on GABAergic interneurons and thalamic/brainstem pathways plausibly dampen seizure‑related confusion and neuroinflammation</cite>.

Pain and procedural sedation:
- Beyond delirium, <cite id="a77aeeb8-0">ketamine reliably reduces postoperative pain and opioid consumption</cite>, which itself lowers delirium risk; this analgesic component should be considered when attributing delirium reductions. 
- In pediatric emergency departments and procedural sedation, <cite id="a77aeeb8-1">ketamine’s rapid onset and efficacy for agitation/delirium are well documented, with reduced delirium incidence reported</cite>.

# Caveats and when benefit is limited

- Heterogeneity and trial quality: <cite id="2efb7124-4">Substantial between‑trial heterogeneity and variable cognitive outcome definitions attenuate pooled benefits; risk of bias in some RCTs undermines certainty</cite>. 
- Psychoactive adverse effects: <cite id="2efb7124-1">Higher subanesthetic doses increase hallucinations and nightmares, potentially worsening perioperative confusion in susceptible patients</cite>. 
- Opioid-sparing vs direct anti-delirium effect: <cite id="a77aeeb8-0">Ketamine’s consistent analgesic and opioid‑sparing effects likely reduce delirium indirectly, but not all studies show a direct preventive effect</cite>. 
- Patient selection and multimodal care: <cite id="2efb7124-4">Subgroup analyses found no consistent advantage by setting, dose, route, or combination with other drugs for delirium prevention, suggesting that standardization and targeted high‑risk strategies are needed</cite>.

# Practical takeaways

- Mechanism-to-clinic: Ketamine’s NMDA antagonism can rebalance cortical excitation–inhibition, dampen seizure‑like hypersynchrony, and mitigate neuroinflammation/excitotoxicity, offering a biological rationale for delirium reduction when dosed briefly and judiciously. <cite id="559b9c4b-0">Improving E/I balance underpins antiseizure effects</cite> <cite id="559b9c4b-1">Acute network disinhibition and chronic hypoactivity provide a biphasic risk/benefit profile</cite> <cite id="559b9c4b-3">Thalamocortical and HCN channel interactions further modulate arousal states</cite>. 
- Setting-specific use: 
  - ICU/general surgery: Consider low-dose, time-limited ketamine as an opioid-sparing adjunct; monitor for psychoactive effects. Expect variable delirium outcomes due to heterogeneity. <cite id="2efb7124-4">No overall preventive effect on delirium</cite> <cite id="2efb7124-0">ICU data suggest potential delirium reduction but are sensitive to study inclusion</cite>. 
  - Cardiac surgery: Early small trials show benefit; larger, pragmatic protocols show no delirium prevention and more hallucinations. Align ketamine with robust nonpharmacologic delirium prevention. <cite id="a77aeeb8-1">Small trial benefits</cite> <cite id="2efb7124-1">PODCAST null results and psychoactive adverse effects</cite>. 
  - Neurosurgery/pediatric ED: Favor neuroprotective and antiseizure mechanisms; integrate ketamine into multimodal sedation/anesthesia plans where appropriate. <cite id="559b9c4b-0">E/I restoration and seizure reduction</cite> <cite id="a77aeeb8-1">Pediatric delirium reduction</cite>. 
- Safety and monitoring: Titrate to the minimum effective dose and avoid sustained subanesthetic exposures that increase hallucinations and nightmares; co‑treat with benzodiazepines or dexmedetomidine as needed, recognizing that some ICU data favor alpha‑2 agonists for delirium prevention. <cite id="2efb7124-1">Ketamine increased hallucinations and nightmares in a dose‑dependent manner</cite> <cite id="2efb7124-4">Meta‑analysis highlights lack of clear delirium prevention benefit and high heterogeneity</cite>.

In sum, ketamine’s NMDA antagonism provides a coherent mechanistic basis for reducing delirium by normalizing cortical and thalamic network dynamics and limiting excitotoxic cascades; in practice, perioperative and ICU studies show heterogeneous but sometimes meaningful reductions in delirium when ketamine is used as a brief, low-dose opioid‑sparing agent, balanced against increased psychoactive adverse effects, with the strongest and most consistent benefits observed in pediatric emergency care and select cardiac surgical protocols. <cite id="559b9c4b-0">Mechanistic restoration of E/I balance underpins antiseizure and neuroprotective effects</cite> <cite id="559b9c4b-1">Acute hyperexcitability and chronic hypoactivity reflect dose/time‑dependent risk profiles</cite> <cite id="2efb7124-4">Perioperative meta‑analysis: no overall delirium prevention</cite> <cite id="2efb7124-1">PODCAST: no delirium prevention with increased hallucinations</cite> <cite id="a77aeeb8-0">Consistent analgesic/opioid‑sparing effects alongside mixed delirium outcomes</cite> <cite id="a77aeeb8-1">Pediatric emergency delirium reductions and early cardiac surgery benefits</cite>.

Title: Intraoperative ketamine does not affect postoperative delirium or pain after major surgery in older adults: an international, multicentre, double-blind, randomised clinical trial
Snippet: Evidence before this study Delirium and pain are both common and serious complications of surgery. These complications cause distress to patients and family members, and are associated with worse postoperative outcomes. Opioids are the mainstay drugs to treat postoperative pain, but also cause delirium and are associated with lifethreatening complications and addiction. At present, there is no pharmacological treatment for delirium. In order to assess the effect of perioperative ketamine on postoperative delirium and pain, we did a systematic search of randomised trials and systematic reviews published in any language. We searched the following databases for studies published up to Feb 5, 2014, (the start of enrolment into the PODCAST trial): MEDLINE, PubMed, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled trials, Web of Science, metaRegister of controlled trials, LILACS, African Health-line, POPLINE, MedCarib, CINAHL, and Clinicaltrials.gov using the following search terms: "ketamine and postoperative delirium" and "ketamine and postoperative pain." The systematic search for "ketamine" and "postoperative delirium" included all randomised controlled trials with surgical patients aged 60 years or older published between 1964 (when ketamine was introduced in clinical practice) and 2014. We identified six studies with a total of 357 patients. Of the six trials, two showed a decrease in delirium with ketamine, one showed an increase in delirium, one had equivocal results, and in two trials there were no patients with delirium. In contrast to the dearth of studies examining the effect of ketamine on postoperative delirium, there have been many studies examining the effect of perioperative ketamine on postoperative pain, with ketamine administered at various doses, at different times, and for variable durations. The vast majority of these studies enrolled fewer than 100 patients, and a few enrolled up to 150 patients. A systematic review of 70 of these trials involving 4701 patients published in 2011 showed that a subanaesthetic dose of ketamine decreased pain for up to 48 h and decreased requirement for opioids after surgery.

Title: Comparison of Ketamine to Haloperidol for Preventing Delirium in ICU Elderly Patients
Snippet: Ketamine, an intravenous anesthetic, is increasingly being used as an alternative agent to treat symptoms of agitation and delirium (19,25,26). Emerging preclinical and clinical research has shown the neuroprotective properties of ketamine (27). A small clinical trial involving cardiac surgery patients showed that administering a low dose of ketamine significantly reduced postoperative delirium without causing any noticeable side effects (28). Moreover, the administration of low-dose ketamine was shown to improve postoperative cognitive impairment following cardiac surgery (29). Furthermore, ketamine has been found to reduce the incidence of emergency delirium in children (30). Ketamine is a safe, fast-acting, and effective treatment for reducing delirium, possibly due to its neuroprotective effects (31). Additionally, ketamine is cost-effective and has been extensively utilized by anesthetists for over six decades. Although there is growing evidence supporting the use of ketamine in delirium prevention, studies are limited, and the current research has not definitively established its efficacy in older hospitalized patients (32). 

There are few studies investigating the efficacy of ketamine as a first-line treatment for elderly patients with delirium (33,34). The present study aimed to investigate the safety and efficacy of administering low-dose ketamine as a potential treatment for reducing delirium in elderly ICU patients. The current study hypothesized that the use of ketamine would be effective in controlling delirium symptoms when compared to the commonly used medication haloperidol. By conducting a randomized clinical trial, this study sought to evaluate the hypothesis and provide insights into the potential benefits of ketamine as a first-line treatment for delirium in elderly patients.

documents.title: Intraoperative ketamine does not affect postoperative delirium or pain after major surgery in older adults: an international, multicentre, double-blind, randomised clinical trial
documents.snippet: Evidence before this study Delirium and pain are both common and serious complications of surgery. These complications cause distress to patients and family members, and are associated with worse postoperative outcomes. Opioids are the mainstay drugs to treat postoperative pain, but also cause delirium and are associated with lifethreatening complications and addiction. At present, there is no pharmacological treatment for delirium. In order to assess the effect of perioperative ketamine on postoperative delirium and pain, we did a systematic search of randomised trials and systematic reviews published in any language. We searched the following databases for studies published up to Feb 5, 2014, (the start of enrolment into the PODCAST trial): MEDLINE, PubMed, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled trials, Web of Science, metaRegister of controlled trials, LILACS, African Health-line, POPLINE, MedCarib, CINAHL, and Clinicaltrials.gov using the following search terms: "ketamine and postoperative delirium" and "ketamine and postoperative pain." The systematic search for "ketamine" and "postoperative delirium" included all randomised controlled trials with surgical patients aged 60 years or older published between 1964 (when ketamine was introduced in clinical practice) and 2014. We identified six studies with a total of 357 patients. Of the six trials, two showed a decrease in delirium with ketamine, one showed an increase in delirium, one had equivocal results, and in two trials there were no patients with delirium. In contrast to the dearth of studies examining the effect of ketamine on postoperative delirium, there have been many studies examining the effect of perioperative ketamine on postoperative pain, with ketamine administered at various doses, at different times, and for variable durations. The vast majority of these studies enrolled fewer than 100 patients, and a few enrolled up to 150 patients. A systematic review of 70 of these trials involving 4701 patients published in 2011 showed that a subanaesthetic dose of ketamine decreased pain for up to 48 h and decreased requirement for opioids after surgery.

documents.title: Comparison of Ketamine to Haloperidol for Preventing Delirium in ICU Elderly Patients
documents.snippet:
Ketamine, an intravenous anesthetic, is increasingly being used as an alternative agent to treat symptoms of agitation and delirium (19,25,26). Emerging preclinical and clinical research has shown the neuroprotective properties of ketamine (27). A small clinical trial involving cardiac surgery patients showed that administering a low dose of ketamine significantly reduced postoperative delirium without causing any noticeable side effects (28). Moreover, the administration of low-dose ketamine was shown to improve postoperative cognitive impairment following cardiac surgery (29). Furthermore, ketamine has been found to reduce the incidence of emergency delirium in children (30). Ketamine is a safe, fast-acting, and effective treatment for reducing delirium, possibly due to its neuroprotective effects (31). Additionally, ketamine is cost-effective and has been extensively utilized by anesthetists for over six decades. Although there is growing evidence supporting the use of ketamine in delirium prevention, studies are limited, and the current research has not definitively established its efficacy in older hospitalized patients (32). 

There are few studies investigating the efficacy of ketamine as a first-line treatment for elderly patients with delirium (33,34). The present study aimed to investigate the safety and efficacy of administering low-dose ketamine as a potential treatment for reducing delirium in elderly ICU patients. The current study hypothesized that the use of ketamine would be effective in controlling delirium symptoms when compared to the commonly used medication haloperidol. By conducting a randomized clinical trial, this study sought to evaluate the hypothesis and provide insights into the potential benefits of ketamine as a first-line treatment for delirium in elderly patients.

Title: Therapeutic potential of ketamine in management of epilepsy: Clinical implications and mechanistic insights.
Snippet: Epilepsy, a widespread neurological disorder, affects approximately 50 million people worldwide. This disorder is typified by recurring seizures due to abnormal neuron communication in the brain. The seizures can lead to severe ischemia and hypoxia, potentially threatening patients' lives. However, with proper diagnosis and treatment, up to 70 % of patients can live without seizures. The causes of epilepsy are complex and multifactorial, encompassing genetic abnormalities, structural brain anomalies, ion channel dysfunctions, neurotransmitter imbalances, neuroinflammation, and immune system involvement. These factors collectively disrupt the crucial balance between excitation and inhibition within the brain, leading to epileptic seizures. The management of treatment-resistant epilepsy remains a considerable challenge, necessitating innovative therapeutic approaches. Among emerging potential treatments, ketamine-a drug traditionally employed for anesthesia and depression-has demonstrated efficacy in reducing seizures. It is noteworthy that, independent of its anti-epileptic effects, ketamine has been found to improve the balance between excitatory and inhibitory (E/I) activities in the brain. The balance is crucial for maintaining normal neural function, and its disruption is widely considered a key driver of epileptic seizures. By acting on N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors and other potential mechanisms, ketamine may regulate neuronal excitability, reduce excessive synchronized neural activity, and counteract epileptic seizures. This positive impact on E/I balance reinforces the potential of ketamine as a promising drug for treating epilepsy, especially in patients who are insensitive to traditional anti-epileptic drugs. This review aims to consolidate the current understanding of ketamine's therapeutic role in epilepsy. It will focus its impact on neuronal excitability and synaptic plasticity, its neuroprotective qualities, and elucidate the drug's potential mechanisms of action in treating epilepsy. By scrutinizing ketamine's impact and mechanisms in various types of epilepsy, we aspire to contribute to a more comprehensive and holistic approach to epilepsy management.

Title: Structural Neurotoxic and Neuroprotective Effects of Ketamine and Esketamine in Preclinical and Human Studies: A Systematic Review
Snippet: The structural neurotoxicity observed with chronic high-dose ketamine exposure likely reflects sustained disruption of excitatory-inhibitory circuit balance downstream of NMDA receptor antagonism. Ketamine preferentially inhibits NMDA receptors on GABAergic interneurons, particularly parvalbumin-positive interneurons, which play a central role in regulating cortical excitation. 105 Suppression of these inhibitory cells leads to disinhibition of pyramidal neurons and a compensatory increase in glutamate release, as reflected by elevated extracellular glutamate levels and increased cortical gamma activity following ketamine administration. 15,57,59,84 While brief glutamate elevations may support adaptive synaptic plasticity and neurotrophic signaling associated with antidepressant effects, repeated or prolonged disinhibition may overwhelm regulatory mechanisms, promoting excitotoxic stress through calcium overload,, mitochondrial dysfunction, and apoptotic signaling. This mechanistic hypothesis aligns with electrophysiological findings in our review, in which acute ketamine consistently enhanced gamma oscillations, reflecting synchronized fast-spiking interneuron activity and cortical hyperexcitability, whereas chronic exposure produced alpha-band slowing and cortical hypoactivity, potentially indicating compensatory downregulation or interneuron dysfunction. 16,57,59 This transition from acute hyperexcitability to chronic hypoactivity mirrors the temporal progression from initial glutamate surge to eventual synaptic depression observed in other excitotoxic paradigms, supporting a biphasic injury model. 106,107

Title: The Role of the NMDA Receptor in the Anticonvulsant Effect of Ellagic Acid in Pentylenetetrazole-Induced Seizures in Male Mice
Snippet: Methods In this experimental study, 64 mice were divided into 8 groups and received the following: normal saline; EA at doses of 6.25, 12.5, and 25 mg/kg; NMDA agonist at a dose of 75 mg/kg; NMDA antagonist (ketamine) at a dose of 0.5 mg/kg; an effective dose of EA plus NMDA agonist; and a subeffective dose of EA plus ketamine. We induced seizure using intravenous administration of PTZ. 60 minutes before induction of seizure, drugs were administrated. Duration lasts to seizure-induced was measured. Finally, the gene expression of NMDA receptor subunits (Nr2a and Nr2b) was assessed in the prefrontal cortex. Results Results showed that EA increased the seizure threshold and decreased the expression of Nr2a and Nr2b. We determined that ketamine potentiated and NMDA attenuated the effects of subeffective and effective doses of EA. Conclusion EA probably via attenuation of the NMDA-R pathway possesses an anticonvulsant effect in PTZ-induced seizure in mice.

Title: Ketamine can produce oscillatory dynamics by engaging mechanisms dependent on the kinetics of NMDA receptors
Snippet: In our work, we showed how NMDA R antagonism in a simple cortical network can give rise to gamma and slow-delta oscillations. However, ketamine can have molecular effects other than NMDA R antagonism. Furthermore, systemic administration of ketamine will affect all structures in the central nervous system. 

The interaction between the cortex, the thalamus and the brainstem can contribute to slow-delta oscillatory dynamics. Indeed, removing significant excitatory input from the brainstem to the cortex can result in slow-delta oscillations [35]. Ketamine can also decrease the activity in excitatory arousal pathways from the parabrachial nucleus and the medial pontine reticular formation in the brainstem to the thalamus and basal forebrain through NMDA R antagonism [36]. The coordination of down-states observed between cortex and thalamus suggests a mechanistic coordination between these two structures [16]. All of these indicate that other slow-delta oscillatory mechanisms can come into play to enhance or complement the mechanisms mediated by NMDA R antagonism at the cortical level. 

Ketamine can also alter hyperpolarization-activated nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels [18] for slowdelta oscillatory contributions. In fact, low doses of ketamine have been found to produce 3 Hz oscillations in posteromedial cortex [3,12]. These 3 Hz oscillations have been found to rely on HCN channels [3]. Ketamine may act on these channels either indirectly through NMDA R antagonism [3] or directly by inhibiting them [18] to produce these oscillations. Again, these mechanisms can enhance or complement the mechanisms mediated by NMDA R antagonism at the cortical level.

Title: Ketamine can produce oscillatory dynamics by engaging mechanisms dependent on the kinetics of NMDA receptors
Snippet: To examine these mechanisms, we developed a biophysical model of a cortical network exposed to ketamine. When we introduce ketamine as an NMDA R antagonist, our model replicates the brain dynamics in human subjects and non-human primates administered ketamine and reveals brain mechanisms underlying the generation of these dynamics. Our model incorporates detailed kinetics for NMDA R dynamics that underlie these mechanisms. By dissecting the model through simulations, we report three advances. 

First, we have established that NMDA R antagonism under ketamine can terminate spiking in active neurons with subthreshold background excitation. We find that, even when NMDA R s are antagonized non-preferentially across all neurons, global disinhibition can emerge when tonic inhibition is provided by interneurons with subthreshold background excitation or high resting membrane potential. Second, we have discovered an NMDA R -dependent mechanism that can generate gamma oscillations in a cortical network, through an interaction between NMDA-and GABA-receptor-mediated currents. As NMDA R closing is known to be slow, this mechanisms stands in contrast to established mechanisms for gamma generation that rely on fast AMPA-and GABA-receptor transmission, such as the pyramidal-interneuronal gamma mechanism [13]. Third, we have discovered an NMDA R -dependent mechanism that can generate slow-delta oscillations in a cortical network, also through an interaction between NMDA-and GABA-receptor-mediated currents. This mechanism relies on an imbalance between excitatory and inhibitory activity, and stands in contrast to established mechanisms for slow-delta generation that rely on membrane channels, such as sodium-activated [14] and ATP-activated [15] potassium channels. 

Through these findings, we explain how the effects of ketamine extend from the subcellular level to the network level to produce the oscillatory dynamics observed in brain activity. Our work proposes new general mechanisms for generating brain dynamics, provides new insight into the mechanism of action of ketamine, and suggests new mechanisms by which ketamine can provide therapeutic effects that go beyond anesthesia, dissociation and analgesia.

Title: The impact of ketamine on outcomes in critically ill patients: a systematic review with meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis of randomized controlled trials
Snippet: In this work, we evaluated the effect of ketamine in critically ill ICU patients. Our meta-analysis of 12 RCTs did not demonstrate differences between ketamine and control groups regarding mortality, pain intensity, opioid or midazolam consumption, and ICU LOS. However, ketamine reduced the delirium rate. This result is significant but may not be robust, and additional RCTs should be conducted in the future. The result on incidences of delirium was sensitive to exclusion of three of four studies, in which case the model showed no difference between the groups. The result on mean opioid consumption was sensitive to exclusion of either one of two studies. For all other outcomes, the result was not sensitive to exclusion of any study. Overall, the results of our study should be used with caution due to the limited number of studies included.

Title: Recent Advances in Preventing and Managing Postoperative Delirium
Snippet: Ketamine has been found to reduce postoperative inflammation 32 , improve perioperative pain outcomes 33 , and reduce excitotoxicity in laboratory models 34 . Results from a small trial also demonstrated decreased occurrence of delirium and decreased incidence of delayed neurocognitive recovery in cardiac surgery patients who received intraoperative ketamine compared with placebo 35,36 . With this background and rationale, an international team of investigators conducted the PODCAST (Prevention of Delirium and Complications Associated with Surgical Treatments) trial, hypothesizing that a sub-anesthetic, intraoperative dose of ketamine would reduce postoperative delirium 37 . In this trial, ketamine had no statistically significant effect on delirium incidence (ketamine groups: 19.45%, placebo group: 19.82%, absolute difference 0.36%, 95% confidence interval [CI] −6.07 to 7.38; P = 0.92), delirium severity, or delirium recurrence 2 . Title: Perioperative ketamine administration to prevent delirium and neurocognitive disorders after surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Snippet: Background: Surgery induces high rates of cognitive disorders, persisting for up to 12 months in elderly adults. This review aimed to assess the currently debated preventive effect of perioperative ketamine on postoperative delirium and postoperative neurocognitive disorders (POND). Materials and methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis including all randomized controlled trials investigating the effects of perioperative ketamine administration in adult patients compared to placebo or no intervention on postoperative delirium and/or POND between January 2007 and April 2022. Database searches were conducted in PubMed, Medline, Embase, Scopus, and Central. Random effects models were used to pool overall estimates. The GRADE approach was used to assess the quality of the evidence. Results: From 1379 records screened, 14 randomized controlled trials with 1618 patients randomized met our inclusion criteria with a high level of consensus among reviewers, amongst whom 50% were at low-moderate risk of bias. There was no between-group difference in postoperative delirium [8 trials, 1265 patients, odds ratio (OR) 0.93, 95% CI (0.51–1.70), I 2=28%] and POND [5 trials, 494 patients, OR 0.52, 95% CI (0.15–1.80); I 2=78%]. There was no significant between-group difference in postoperative psychological adverse effects, level of pain, hospital length of stay, or mortality. Between-group subgroup analyses showed no difference in delirium or POND incidence according to surgical setting, ketamine dose, mode of administration, combination or not with other drug(s), and assessment timing or definition of cognitive disorders. Conclusion: Perioperative ketamine does not prevent postoperative delirium or POND. Significant study heterogeneity suggests that standardized measures for POND assessment and a specific focus on patients at high risk for POND should be used to improve the comparability of future studies.

Short answer

Ketamine’s effects are dose-dependent: lower-dose infusions provide analgesia with limited sedation, while higher doses increase sedation and produce prominent dissociative, hallucinatory, and psychotic symptoms, which are most common at doses ≥1 mg/kg/hr; these psychiatric symptoms can trigger agitation, confusion with visual disturbances, and mixed delirium presentations, especially when combined with opioids and when patients are arousable enough to exhibit psychomotor hyperactivity <cite id="a1be6498-2">Ketamine’s pharmacology is dose-dependent; analgesia at 0.1–0.4 mg/kg/hr, sedation at 0.4–1.0 mg/kg/hr; undesirable psychiatric symptoms including psychosis and hallucinations are most common at doses ≥1 mg/kg/hr</cite>. Title: Precision‐based approaches to delirium in critical illness: A narrative review
Snippet: In 2018, Krewulak et al. 2 reported a systematic review and metaanalysis summarizing the existing literature on the incidence and prevalence of delirium subtypes in the ICU. The authors reported additional variables that contributed to the heterogeneity of the ICU population. 

Studies that used the RASS and CAM-ICU defined hypoactive delirium as a positive CAM-ICU assessment associated with a RASS score of 0 to −3. Hyperactive delirium was defined as a positive CAM-ICU associated with a daily RASS score of +1 to +4. Mixed delirium was defined as a positive CAM-ICU assessment and a daily RASS score that fluctuated between hypoactive and hyperactive delirium. Incidence was defined as new cases of delirium in intensive care and prevalence was defined as existing cases. 2 The pooled incidence of delirium psychomotor subtypes was reported in 18 studies: hyperactive (4% [95% CI, 2-6; I 2 (measure of study heterogeneity) = 92%]), hypoactive (11% [95% CI, 8-17; I 2 = 97%]), and mixed (7% [95% CI, 4-11; I 2 = 97%]). Thirty-one studies reported delirium prevalence; delirium psychomotor subtypes were hyperactive (4% [95% CI, 3-6; I 2 = 94%]), hypoactive (17% [95% CI, 13-22; I = 97%]), and mixed (10% [95% CI, 6-16; I 2 = 99%]). The pooled prevalence of hypoactive delirium in a sicker subset (as defined by higher severity of illness and receipt of mechanical ventilation) was higher than the pooled prevalence of hypoactive delirium among the entire study population (35% [95% CI, 23-55%] I 2 = 93% versus 29% [95% CI, 18-46%] I 2 = 95%, respectfully).

Title: Delirium in critically ill COVID-19 patients: incidence, predictors, and outcomes in invasive mechanical ventilation with versus without ECMO support
Snippet: A critical aspect often insufficiently addressed in ICU delirium research is the heterogeneity of delirium motor subtypes, which include hypoactive, hyperactive, and mixed forms. Hypoactive delirium, characterized by reduced motor activity, lethargy, and diminished responsiveness, frequently goes underdiagnosed due to its subtle clinical presentation but is associated with poor outcomes equal to or worse than hyperactive delirium [23]. Given the retrospective nature of our assessment, relying mainly on chart review and CAM-ICU documentation, underrecognition of hypoactive delirium is a plausible limitation. Differentiating delirium subtypes prospectively would enhance risk stratification and inform precise therapeutic approaches, since sedation regimens and mobilization strategies may differentially impact the prevalence and severity of delirium subtypes.

Title: Inattentive Delirium vs. Disorganized Thinking: A New Axis to Subcategorize PACU Delirium
Snippet: Of the 229 patients who had had the CAM-ICU test completed, 35 patients (15%) failed the attention section of the CAM-ICU test (see Figure 1). Of these, three patients showed a calm and alert level of arousal (RASS = 0), and only one of these three patients failed the disorganized thinking section of the CAM-ICU and received the diagnosis of delirium. Of the remaining 32 patients showing inattention with altered levels of arousal (a RASS lower or higher than zero) thus screening positive for a motoric subtype of delirium, 25 showed inattention with low arousal (RASS <0, sub-diagnosed with hypoactive delirium), and seven showed inattention with high arousal (RASS >0, sub-diagnosed with hyperactive delirium). Title: Delirium in Intensive Care
Snippet: 3 clinical subclasses: hyperactive, hypoactive and mixed motor subtype based on the predominant psychomotor activity. The hypoactive patient has slowed mentation, lethargy, and decreased movements, while the hyperactive patient has an increased number of spontaneous movements that are purposeless, uncontrollable, and inefficient. A delirious patient may fluctuate between a hypoactive and hyperactive state and the delirium is then termed mixed form [4]. While hyperactive motor subtype is the easiest to detect in clinical practice it is the least prevalent. Hypoactive motor subtype is the most common motor subtype in the ICU but is easily overlooked due to its silent clinical picture [5].

Short answer
Across ICU studies using ketamine for analgosedation, ketamine exposure is associated with higher overall delirium risk, but when delirium occurs, hyperactive, hypoactive, and mixed subtypes are distributed similarly to patients receiving other sedatives, with no consistent evidence that ketamine preferentially produces hyperactive versus hypoactive delirium; higher ketamine doses and co-drugs (e.g., antipsychotics) correlate with more psychiatric side effects and may favor agitation/mixed presentations, whereas lower-dose analgosedation strategies reduce sedation depth and delirium burden <cite id="a1be6498-2">Ketamine increases risk for incident ICU delirium, with psychiatric symptoms (hallucinations/psychosis) most common at doses ≥1 mg/kg/hr</cite><cite id="a1be6498-2">Analgesic predominates at 0.1–0.4 mg/kg/hr and sedative effects appear at 0.4–1.0 mg/kg/hr</cite><cite id="a1be6498-0">Hyperactive delirium was defined as +CAM-ICU with RASS > 0 or scheduled antipsychotic use; hypoactive as +CAM-ICU with RASS ≤ 0; mixed if both</cite><cite id="a1be6498-2">In patients who developed delirium, motoric subtypes and other risks/treatments were similar between ketamine and nonketamine groups, except higher opioid use and urgent surgical ICU admission among ketamine-delirium patients</cite><cite id="74417d8f-0">Across ICU studies, hyperactive delirium pooled incidence 4%, hypoactive 11%, mixed 7% by CAM-ICU+RASS criteria</cite>.

What delirium subtypes mean and how they are measured in ICU
ICU delirium is commonly subclassified into hyperactive, hypoactive, and mixed based on CAM-ICU positivity combined with daily RASS: hyperactive denotes agitation with RASS +1 to +4, hypoactive denotes reduced activity with RASS 0 to −3, and mixed denotes fluctuation between these states; incidence (new cases) and prevalence (existing cases) vary across studies but typically show hypoactive as the most common subtype while hyperactive is least prevalent and often underrecognized <cite id="74417d8f-0">Studies using RASS and CAM-ICU defined hyperactive as +CAM-ICU with RASS +1 to +4, hypoactive as +CAM-ICU with RASS 0 to −3, mixed as fluctuating between; pooled incidence hyperactive 4%, hypoactive 11%, mixed 7%</cite><cite id="74417d8f-4">Delirium subclasses: hyperactive shows increased movements; hypoactive shows slowed mentation and decreased movement; mixed fluctuates between</cite><cite id="74417d8f-4">Hypoactive is often most common in ICU but easily overlooked; hyperactive easiest to detect but least prevalent</cite>. In practice, antipsychotic use during delirium can be used alongside CAM-ICU to flag hyperactive phenotypes, and lower RASS indicates hypoactivity <cite id="a1be6498-0">Hyperactive defined as +CAM-ICU with RASS > 0 or scheduled antipsychotic use; hypoactive as +CAM-ICU with RASS ≤ 0</cite>.

Observational evidence on ketamine and delirium motoric subtypes
A large single-center cohort (RadboudUMC) compared ICU patients receiving ketamine analgosedation versus those not receiving ketamine, with daily CAM-ICU screening and RASS-based motoric subtyping. Ketamine exposure was associated with an increased risk of incident delirium overall; among patients who did develop delirium, motoric subtypes (hyperactive, hypoactive, mixed) were broadly similar between ketamine and nonketamine groups, with the exception that ketamine-delirium patients more often received opioids and were more likely to be in urgent surgery, and they more often received scheduled antipsychotics, which by definition label delirium as hyperactive on this operationalization <cite id="a1be6498-1">Ketamine analgosedation may increase delirium risk; mechanisms unclear; prospective randomized trials needed</cite><cite id="a1be6498-2">Despite increased delirium risk with ketamine, when delirium occurred, age, coma, opioid and benzodiazepine use independently increased risk; among delirious patients, motoric subtypes, other risk factors, treatments, and outcomes were similar between ketamine and nonketamine groups, except urgent surgery and greater opioid/IV clonidine exposure; median ketamine dose for delirious patients was 0.5 mg/kg/hr; psychiatric side effects peak at ≥1 mg/kg/hr</cite><cite id="a1be6498-0">Subtyping used for analysis: hyperactive (+CAM-ICU with RASS > 0 or scheduled antipsychotic), hypoactive (+CAM-ICU with RASS ≤ 0), mixed</cite>. Another ICU cohort in mechanically ventilated COPD patients using continuous ketamine 4 μg/kg/min reported 12% delirium during the analyzed period with no ketamine-attributed adverse events; while not a head-to-head comparator, it suggests feasibility and relatively low delirium incidence in a specific cohort and again highlights the need to consider dose and clinical context <cite id="a1be6498-3">Continuous ketamine 4 μg/kg/min in ventilated COPD patients: 12% delirium during ICU stay, no ketamine-attributed AEs</cite>. Across ICU delirium literature, hypoactive delirium is more prevalent and underrecognized, and mixed delirium is common; this provides context for interpreting subtype distributions under ketamine <cite id="74417d8f-0">Pooled incidence: hypoactive 11%, hyperactive 4%, mixed 7%</cite><cite id="74417d8f-2">Hypoactive delirium is frequent, underdiagnosed, and has outcomes equal to or worse than hyperactive; prospective subtype differentiation is needed</cite>.

Pharmacology and dose-dependent risk phenotypes
Ketamine’s effects are dose-dependent: lower-dose infusions provide analgesia with limited sedation, while higher doses increase sedation and produce prominent dissociative, hallucinatory, and psychotic symptoms, which are most common at doses ≥1 mg/kg/hr; these psychiatric symptoms can trigger agitation, confusion with visual disturbances, and mixed delirium presentations, especially when combined with opioids and when patients are arousable enough to exhibit psychomotor hyperactivity <cite id="a1be6498-2">Ketamine’s pharmacology is dose-dependent; analgesia at 0.1–0.4 mg/kg/hr, sedation at 0.4–1.0 mg/kg/hr; undesirable psychiatric symptoms including psychosis and hallucinations are most common at doses ≥1 mg/kg/hr</cite>. In practice, ketamine’s lack of respiratory depression and hemodynamic instability makes it attractive for analgosedation, yet its potential for delirium correlates with dose and co-medication exposure, including benzodiazepines and antipsychotics, which shape subtype labeling (e.g., antipsychotic use implies hyperactive delirium by cohort criteria) <cite id="a1be6498-2">Ketamine has advantages over opioids/propofol (less respiratory depression, lower hypotension risk); undesirable psychiatric symptoms increase at higher doses</cite><cite id="a1be6498-2">Ketamine-delirium patients received more opioid and IV clonidine; more received scheduled antipsychotics, which by definition marks hyperactive subtype</cite>.

Head-to-head comparator evidence
A randomized clinical trial in elderly non-intubated ICU patients compared low-dose ketamine and dexmedetomidine for sedation and delirium prevention; the study found no significant difference in delirium incidence or within-group severity at 60 minutes, with primary outcomes focused on time to adequate sedation (RASS ≤ +1). Although this trial did not report motoric subtypes directly, the lack of difference in delirium incidence suggests ketamine does not inherently drive a distinct hyperactive versus hypoactive phenotype relative to an α2-adrenergic sedative in this population, and the observed psychiatric adverse effects were not superior to dexmedetomidine in the short term <cite id="b64d18fa-0">No significant difference in delirium between low-dose ketamine and dexmedetomidine in elderly non-intubated ICU patients after 60 minutes; primary outcome was % achieving RASS ≤ +1</cite><cite id="b64d18fa-1">Trial randomized elderly ICU patients to ketamine 20 mg or dexmedetomidine 0.2 μg/kg/h titrated; no significant intergroup delirium difference reported at 60 minutes</cite>. Broader ICU evidence shows that hypoactive delirium is often underrecognized and carries high risk, emphasizing the need to monitor across subtypes and to consider sedation strategies that avoid both deep sedation (which can unmask hypoactive states) and arousable agitation (which can mask delirium or drive mixed presentations) <cite id="74417d8f-2">Underrecognition of hypoactive delirium is common and outcomes are equal to or worse than hyperactive</cite><cite id="a1be6498-0">Hyperactive delirium in this cohort was defined by CAM-ICU plus RASS > 0 or antipsychotics, reflecting clinical management</cite>.

Clinical implications and remaining uncertainties
- Practical inference: Ketamine increases overall delirium risk in ICU populations, particularly at higher infusion doses and in the presence of opioids or antipsychotics, which may bias toward agitation/mixed phenotypes by virtue of antipsychotic use; however, when delirium occurs under ketamine versus other sedatives, motoric subtypes are generally similar, and hypoactive and mixed delirium remain common and underrecognized across regimens <cite id="a1be6498-2">Ketamine increases delirium risk; higher-dose ketamine associates with more psychiatric symptoms</cite><cite id="a1be6498-2">Among delirious patients, motoric subtypes and treatments were similar between ketamine and nonketamine groups, except more opioid and antipsychotic exposure in ketamine-delirium cases</cite><cite id="74417d8f-0">Across studies, hypoactive delirium incidence 11% and mixed 7%, with high heterogeneity</cite>. 
- Mechanistic expectation: Because ketamine can produce hallucinations and psychosis at higher doses, one might expect more mixed or hyperactive features during periods of adequate arousal; at lower doses used for analgosedation, sedation depth is reduced and delirium, when present, may be more likely to be hypoactive or mixed due to inattention with low arousal, similar to other sedatives <cite id="a1be6498-2">Psychiatric side effects peak at ≥1 mg/kg/hr; analgesia at 0.1–0.4 mg/kg/hr and sedation at 0.4–1.0 mg/kg/hr</cite><cite id="74417d8f-0">Subtype definitions by RASS and CAM-ICU</cite>. 
- Evidence gaps: Few studies report motoric subtypes stratified by ketamine exposure relative to propofol or benzodiazepines, and most are observational or short-term RCTs without routine subtype telemetry. Prospective studies that continuously monitor arousal and attention with standardized subtype documentation are needed to determine whether ketamine exposure shifts the balance between hypoactive, hyperactive, or mixed delirium, independent of dose and co-drug effects <cite id="a1be6498-1">Prospective randomized trials are needed to quantify delirium magnitude and characterize psychiatric symptoms during ketamine therapy</cite><cite id="74417d8f-2">Prospective differentiation of subtypes is needed to refine stratification and therapy</cite>.

Bottom line
Available ICU evidence does not support a consistent, dose-independent bias of ketamine toward hyperactive versus hypoactive delirium. Ketamine increases overall delirium risk, particularly at higher doses and with co-drug exposure, and when delirium occurs, hyperactive, hypoactive, and mixed subtypes are distributed similarly to other sedatives; higher doses and antipsychotic use can inflate the apparent hyperactive count in cohorts that label antipsychotic-treated delirium as hyperactive. Clinicians should anticipate a spectrum of subtypes under ketamine, monitor with CAM-ICU and RASS, minimize high-dose exposure and antipsychotic reliance where possible, and recognize that hypoactive delirium remains common and underrecognized with significant outcomes risk <cite id="a1be6498-2">Ketamine increases delirium risk and psychiatric symptoms at higher doses; among delirious patients, motoric subtypes were similar to nonketamine comparators, except for opioid/antipsychotic exposure</cite><cite id="a1be6498-0">Subtypes defined by CAM-ICU with RASS thresholds and antipsychotic use</cite><cite id="74417d8f-0">Pooled ICU subtype incidence: hyperactive 4%, hypoactive 11%, mixed 7%</cite><cite id="b64d18fa-0">No significant intergroup delirium difference ketamine vs dexmedetomidine in elderly non-intubated ICU patients at 60 minutes</cite><cite id="74417d8f-2">Hypoactive delirium underrecognized and carries poor outcomes equal to or worse than hyperactive</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Exploring Ketamine Analgosedation Use and Its Effect on Incident Delirium in Critically Ill Adults
Snippet: In conclusion, our study suggests ketamine analgosedation in critically ill surgical and medical adults may contribute to an increased risk for incident ICU delirium. Despite the extensive comparative analyses conducted between the ketamine and nonketamine groups who developed delirium, the mechanisms for delirium in patients receiving ketamine analgesedation remain unclear. Future, well-designed, prospective, randomized trials are needed to carefully evaluate the magnitude of delirium risk associated ketamine analgosedation and whether psychiatric symptoms observed during ketamine therapy truly represent delirium.

Title: Exploring Ketamine Analgosedation Use and Its Effect on Incident Delirium in Critically Ill Adults
Snippet: Our results suggest ketamine, when administered to critically ill surgical and medical patients requiring analgosedation, may increase the risk for ICU incident delirium. Age, coma, opioid use, and benzodiazepine use were also each independently associated with a greater delirium risk. With the exception that patients admitted to the ICU for urgent surgery were more likely to develop delirium with ketamine and more ketamine patients with delirium received opioid and IV clonidine therapy, other delirium risks, motorotic subtypes, treatments, and ICU outcomes were similar between the ketamine and nonketamine patients who developed delirium. 

Ketamine, with its lack of effect on respiratory drive and low propensity to cause hypotension or coma, has advantages over opioids and propofol in critically ill adults requiring analgosedation (1, 2). Ketamine is increasingly being used to optimize ICU patient comfort and safety (3) despite the current lack of a large, multicenter, controlled trial evaluating its analgosedation safety and efficacy (3). The pharmacology of ketamine is complex, and dose-dependent: analgesic effects usually predominate at lower doses (0.1-0.4 mg/kg/hr) and sedative effects at higher doses (0.4-1.0 mg/kg/hr) (1, 2). 

The ketamine patients in our analysis who developed delirium received a median ketamine infusion dose of 0.5 mg/kg/hr-a dose similar to that reported in other ketamine analgosedation studies (9,11,12). The undesirable psychiatric symptoms of ketamine including psychosis and hallucinations are most common at doses greater than or equal to 1 mg/kg/hr (7).

The pharmacology of ketamine is complex, and dose-dependent: analgesic effects usually predominate at lower doses (0.1-0.4 mg/kg/hr) and sedative effects at higher doses (0.4-1.0 mg/kg/hr) (1, 2). 

The ketamine patients in our analysis who developed delirium received a median ketamine infusion dose of 0.5 mg/kg/hr-a dose similar to that reported in other ketamine analgosedation studies (9,11,12). The undesirable psychiatric symptoms of ketamine including psychosis and hallucinations are most common at doses greater than or equal to 1 mg/kg/hr (7).

Title: Precision‐based approaches to delirium in critical illness: A narrative review
Snippet: In 2018, Krewulak et al. 2 reported a systematic review and metaanalysis summarizing the existing literature on the incidence and prevalence of delirium subtypes in the ICU. The authors reported additional variables that contributed to the heterogeneity of the ICU population. 

Studies that used the RASS and CAM-ICU defined hypoactive delirium as a positive CAM-ICU assessment associated with a RASS score of 0 to −3. Hyperactive delirium was defined as a positive CAM-ICU associated with a daily RASS score of +1 to +4. Mixed delirium was defined as a positive CAM-ICU assessment and a daily RASS score that fluctuated between hypoactive and hyperactive delirium. Incidence was defined as new cases of delirium in intensive care and prevalence was defined as existing cases. 2 The pooled incidence of delirium psychomotor subtypes was reported in 18 studies: hyperactive (4% [95% CI, 2-6; I 2 (measure of study heterogeneity) = 92%]), hypoactive (11% [95% CI, 8-17; I 2 = 97%]), and mixed (7% [95% CI, 4-11; I 2 = 97%]). Thirty-one studies reported delirium prevalence; delirium psychomotor subtypes were hyperactive (4% [95% CI, 3-6; I 2 = 94%]), hypoactive (17% [95% CI, 13-22; I = 97%]), and mixed (10% [95% CI, 6-16; I 2 = 99%]). The pooled prevalence of hypoactive delirium in a sicker subset (as defined by higher severity of illness and receipt of mechanical ventilation) was higher than the pooled prevalence of hypoactive delirium among the entire study population (35% [95% CI, 23-55%] I 2 = 93% versus 29% [95% CI, 18-46%] I 2 = 95%, respectfully).
