Title: Inattentive Delirium vs. Disorganized Thinking: A New Axis to Subcategorize PACU Delirium
Snippet: Of the 229 patients who had had the CAM-ICU test completed, 35 patients (15%) failed the attention section of the CAM-ICU test (see Figure 1). Of these, three patients showed a calm and alert level of arousal (RASS = 0), and only one of these three patients failed the disorganized thinking section of the CAM-ICU and received the diagnosis of delirium. Of the remaining 32 patients showing inattention with altered levels of arousal (a RASS lower or higher than zero) thus screening positive for a motoric subtype of delirium, 25 showed inattention with low arousal (RASS <0, sub-diagnosed with hypoactive delirium), and seven showed inattention with high arousal (RASS >0, sub-diagnosed with hyperactive delirium). Patients with inattentive delirium had undergone longer operations (median operation length 116 vs. 87 min, p = 0.028).

Title: Delirium in Intensive Care
Snippet: 3 clinical subclasses: hyperactive, hypoactive and mixed motor subtype based on the predominant psychomotor activity. The hypoactive patient has slowed mentation, lethargy, and decreased movements, while the hyperactive patient has an increased number of spontaneous movements that are purposeless, uncontrollable, and inefficient. A delirious patient may fluctuate between a hypoactive and hyperactive state and the delirium is then termed mixed form [4]. While hyperactive motor subtype is the easiest to detect in clinical practice it is the least prevalent. Hypoactive motor subtype is the most common motor subtype in the ICU but is easily overlooked due to its silent clinical picture [5].

Incidence was defined as new cases of delirium in intensive care and prevalence was defined as existing cases. 2 The pooled incidence of delirium psychomotor subtypes was reported in 18 studies: hyperactive (4% [95% CI, 2-6; I 2 (measure of study heterogeneity) = 92%]), hypoactive (11% [95% CI, 8-17; I 2 = 97%]), and mixed (7% [95% CI, 4-11; I 2 = 97%]). Thirty-one studies reported delirium prevalence; delirium psychomotor subtypes were hyperactive (4% [95% CI, 3-6; I 2 = 94%]), hypoactive (17% [95% CI, 13-22; I = 97%]), and mixed (10% [95% CI, 6-16; I 2 = 99%]). The pooled prevalence of hypoactive delirium in a sicker subset (as defined by higher severity of illness and receipt of mechanical ventilation) was higher than the pooled prevalence of hypoactive delirium among the entire study population (35% [95% CI, 23-55%] I 2 = 93% versus 29% [95% CI, 18-46%] I 2 = 95%, respectfully).

snippet.text: A critical aspect often insufficiently addressed in ICU delirium research is the heterogeneity of delirium motor subtypes, which include hypoactive, hyperactive, and mixed forms. Hypoactive delirium, characterized by reduced motor activity, lethargy, and diminished responsiveness, frequently goes underdiagnosed due to its subtle clinical presentation but is associated with poor outcomes equal to or worse than hyperactive delirium [23]. Given the retrospective nature of our assessment, relying mainly on chart review and CAM-ICU documentation, underrecognition of hypoactive delirium is a plausible limitation. Differentiating delirium subtypes prospectively would enhance risk stratification and inform precise therapeutic approaches, since sedation regimens and mobilization strategies may differentially impact the prevalence and severity of delirium subtypes.

snippet.text: Of the 229 patients who had had the CAM-ICU test completed, 35 patients (15%) failed the attention section of the CAM-ICU test (see Figure 1). Of these, three patients showed a calm and alert level of arousal (RASS = 0), and only one of these three patients failed the disorganized thinking section of the CAM-ICU and received the diagnosis of delirium. Of the remaining 32 patients showing inattention with altered levels of arousal (a RASS lower or higher than zero) thus screening positive for a motoric subtype of delirium, 25 showed inattention with low arousal (RASS <0, sub-diagnosed with hypoactive delirium), and seven showed inattention with high arousal (RASS >0, sub-diagnosed with hyperactive delirium). The hypoactive patient has slowed mentation, lethargy, and decreased movements, while the hyperactive patient has an increased number of spontaneous movements that are purposeless, uncontrollable, and inefficient. A delirious patient may fluctuate between a hypoactive and hyperactive state and the delirium is then termed mixed form [4]. While hyperactive motor subtype is the easiest to detect in clinical practice it is the least prevalent. Hypoactive motor subtype is the most common motor subtype in the ICU but is easily overlooked due to its silent clinical picture [5].

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer does NOT satisfy the verification criterion. The criterion requires the answer to explicitly state that the ketamine-delirium literature does NOT systematically distinguish hyperactive versus hypoactive subtypes in outcome assessment, and that standard screening tools (CAM-ICU, ICDSC) detect presence/absence without reliably phenotyping motor presentation. Instead, the answer presents detailed analysis of subtype distributions under ketamine exposure (e.g., 'when delirium occurs, hyperactive, hypoactive, and mixed subtypes are distributed similarly to patients receiving other sedatives') as though subtype-stratified data exists and supports these conclusions. While the answer mentions in the 'Evidence gaps' section that 'Few studies report motoric subtypes stratified by ketamine exposure,' this acknowledgment is buried and does not come close to the explicit, prominent statement required by the criterion. The answer reads as if subtype-specific analyses have been conducted and support the claims being made, when in fact the literature does not systematically assess ketamine's differential effects on delirium subtypes. The single observational study [1] that attempted subtype classification used a non-standard definition (antipsychotic use as a marker of hyperactive delirium), which the answer acknowledges but does not treat as a fundamental limitation precluding conclusions about differential subtype effects.
other_issues: The answer conflates subtype measurement methodology with actual subtype-stratified outcome data. Reference [1] used a post-hoc subtype classification scheme (RASS thresholds + antipsychotic use), but the answer treats this as evidence that 'motoric subtypes...were similar between ketamine and nonketamine groups' without clearly stating this is a single observational study with major confounding (antipsychotic use defines the subtype).

The answer presents mechanistic speculation ('Because ketamine can produce hallucinations and psychosis at higher doses, one might expect more mixed or hyperactive features...') in a way that could be misread as empirically supported, though it does preface with 'Mechanistic expectation.'

The 'Bottom line' states 'Available ICU evidence does not support a consistent, dose-independent bias of ketamine toward hyperactive versus hypoactive delirium'—this frames the issue as if the evidence has been examined and found not to support differential effects, rather than acknowledging the evidence does not exist because studies don't systematically phenotype subtypes in ketamine research.

Reference [4] reports 12% delirium incidence in COPD patients receiving ketamine, but no subtype data; the answer uses this to suggest 'feasibility and relatively low delirium incidence' without noting this tells us nothing about subtypes.

The answer repeatedly cites pooled subtype incidence data from reference [2] (hyperactive 4%, hypoactive 11%, mixed 7%) as if this provides context for ketamine-specific effects, but reference [2] is a general ICU delirium review not focused on ketamine, so these numbers don't inform the question.

The RCT comparing ketamine to dexmedetomidine [6,7] found no difference in delirium incidence but did not report subtypes at all; the answer infers from this that ketamine 'does not inherently drive a distinct hyperactive versus hypoactive phenotype,' which is an unsupported extrapolation from absence of data.
judgment.summary: The answer fails the verification criterion by presenting observational and mechanistic analyses as though they constitute evidence for how ketamine differentially affects delirium subtypes, rather than explicitly stating that the literature does not systematically distinguish subtypes in ketamine studies. The answer treats a single observational study's post-hoc subtype classification (with major methodological confounding) as sufficient to conclude subtypes are 'similar' between ketamine and control groups, and buries the acknowledgment of evidence gaps rather than leading with the fundamental limitation that CAM-ICU/RASS-based tools don't reliably phenotype motor presentations and ketamine studies don't stratify outcomes by subtype.
